speechtext:

My motion is prompted by the do-nothing budgeting of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) for one million unemployed. In view of the fact that in government waste there lie fallow immense resources for creating and stimulating employment, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski):
That this House directs the Minister of Finance to make a statement on motions at the earliest possible opportunity to explain what steps he is taking to reassess and reallocate government funds now in unessential programs to the battle against unemployment.

That the whole matter of icebreaker service to the fishing industry be referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications and the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry.

subsubtopic: MR. RODRIGUEZ-UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-MINISTER'S STATEMENTS ON WITHHOLDING BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to raise what 1 consider to be a matter of privilege stemming from statements by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) concerning the withholding of unemployment insurance benefits from people who were over 65 and those who were on dependency benefits at the time of the implementation of Bill C-69 on January 1, 1976. I feel I was deliberately misled by responses from the minister to questions I raised both in this House and in the committee, and that the misleading nature of the minister's statements seriously interfered not only with my capacity to act as a member of parliament but also with the work of all other members of parliament both in this House and more specifically in the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and immigration.
My concern in this regard arises from the following incidents. I was very concerned about the fact that 18,000 people over age 65 were having certain benefits withheld from them by the Unemployment Insurance Commission, because I felt the commission had the authority to make the necessary payments. Because of this concern 1 raised a question in the House on April 5, 1977, which is recorded at page 4643 of Hansard. 1 will read the question and the minister's response. The question was as follows:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the minister responsible for unemployment. In view of the fact that 18,000 people were unjustly disentitled from unemployment insurance benefits because they were over the age of 65 when Bill C-69 came into effect, and in view of the fact that the minister told this House on February 10 that he was satisfied with information from the Department of Justice that it would not be necessary to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act in order for these people to be paid the money owing to them, could the minister tell the House why his department is now refusing to make those payments?
The minister replied as follows:
Mr. Speaker, as I have indicated, given the numbers to which the hon. member has referred, it did seem appropriate to take, as we did take, the necessary step of contacting the individuals personally to see whether they do in fact qualify. Justice indicated that we had the authority, but so that there will be no doubt we propose to suggest an amendment at the committee stage of the bill.
The minister indicated clearly in that statement that he had been informed by the Department of Justice that his department did, indeed, have the authority to make the necessary payments. In order to clear up the matter further, I asked the following supplementary question:
A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. In view of the fact that when these people do go to their local office and apply for benefits they are being told by officers of the minister's department that an amendment must be made to the Unemployment Insurance Act, would the minister promise the House that he will inform the minions in the local offices that they are to process the applications of these people so they can obtain their benefits?
Unfortunately, the minister refused to answer that question then, so I elected to pursue the matter further in the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration which was dealing with the estimates of the minister's department with respect to the U1C. A meeting was held that very afternoon at
Privilege-Mr. Rodriguez
3.30, and I was there. I would like to read the Minutes of an exchange which took place in that committee at page 11:6. I put the same questions to the minister in the committee as follows:
Madam Chairman, 1 want to start off by following up a question I asked the minister in the House today with respect to those 18,000 people aged 65 who were collecting unemployment insurance benefits at the time C-69 came into effect in January of 1976. The minister told us in the House that from the advice he has gotten from the Department of Justice there is no need for any amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act for those people to get what is justly theirs and what the courts ruled is theirs. Now, in the local offices they are being told-and I had a case just last week-it is a lot of B.S., that an amendment has to be made to the act and this decision is going to be pending, et cetera, blah, blah, ad nauseam.
Can the minister clarify this matter so that information can be given to these people?
This is what the minister replied:
Yes, the original advice that we had, from Justice, Mr. Rodriguez, was to the effect that we in fact did not need an amendment to C-27 but in the interests of caution, I guess, for want of a better word, and so that it was not open to challenge, there was a feeling that we should in fact look to an amendment at the committee stage of the bill. I understand, and 1 just got this information today, that Justice have since fortified their original decision, namely, that we do not need an amendment to the bill, so that we can proceed, notwithstanding whether 1 do or do not choose to move an amendment at the committee stage.
I followed with another question which was as follows:
So, Madam Chairman, can the minister give me and the committee the assurance that the local offices will be informed to process these applications rather than putting them off any further?
This was the minister's answer:
1 will ask Mr. Charlebois to comment on the logistics of it, Mr. Rodriguez.
Mr, J. Y. C. Charlebois, deputy executive director of the Unemployment Insurance Commission, got into the act and said:
Madam Chairman, what the minister has just indicated to the committee was information that was given to us just yesterday so the instructions that were given to the field a few weeks ago will have to be changed. This has not been done yet and we will make sure that instructions are issued as soon as possible so that the claims that are being reviewed can be processed right away.
The statements of the minister were clear and not at all open to interpretation. He said in the House of Commons that the Department of Justice indicated that he had the authority to make the payments to the 18,000 people 1 referred to in my questions. That afternoon he told me and the other members of the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration that on that very day the Department of Justice had fortified its original decision, which was as follows:
Namely, that we do not need an amendment to the bill, so that we can proceed, notwithstanding whether 1 do or do not choose to move an amendment at committee stage.
The minister's statements are crystal clear, Mr. Speaker. There is also no question in my mind that what is involved is not a slip of the tongue, considering the fact that the minister had received such information that very day and that it was supported in the committee by top officials-not the little third-class and fourth-class echelon people, but the top officials of his department who were there to advise him.

April 19, 1977
Privilege-Mr. Rodriguez
Acting on the basis of information the minister supplied to me, 1 spoke to members of the press and to individuals in my riding, as well as to those who were advocating the cause of these people and were actively working on this matter. 1 informed them of the minister's exact words which indicated that these people would soon be receiving their payments. Two days later, on Thursday, April 7, I received a letter from the minister. The letter had not been signed, but had been forwarded to me in that condition by the senior assistant deputy minister, Mr. J. L. Manion. The letter reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Rodriguez:
I am writing in connection with the questions you raised in the House and in the standing committee on Tuesday, April 5, 1977, regarding claimants aged 65 and over and claimants eligible for the dependency rate of benefit who were affected by Bill C-69. Your concern was whether we needed to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act in order to make payments to these claimants. I feel that the remarks that I and my officials made may not have left the correct impression and I therefore wish to clarify the facts of the situation.
There are three points, Mr. Speaker. The second point is extremely important and I should like to read it into the record. The second point in the minister's unsigned letter reads as follows:
We received legal advice to the effect that an amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act was required to implement our decision to pay the claimants who did not appeal but who were in the same position as the appellants. An amendment is contained in clause 48 of Bill C-27 to clarify the commission's powers to reconsider claims. It would be our intention to use the amended authority in C-27 to make the payments to the claimants who did not appeal, subject to final legal confirmation that the amended section can be applied retroactively. If not, a further redrafting of the amendment would be proposed to ensure its applicability to the claimants in question.
Mr. Speaker, first of all, in the House the minister said that the Department of Justice told him that he had the authority to pay. Just yesterday in the committee he said that the department had fortified the decision and that an amendment was not needed in order to pay. In his letter to me two days after the committee appearance, when he found he could not contact me by telephone, in point No. 2 of his letter he said that he needed authority to make retroactive payments. That letter contradicts the minister's statements in the House and in committee, Mr. Speaker. It is not a matter of remarks having left the correct impression; it is a matter of complete contradiction in two statements.
1 believe the minister is deliberately misleading myself and the House in one or both of these statements. On one day we are told that the minister has just received information from the Department of Justice indicating that it is reaffirming its position that payments can be made. Two days later he says exactly the opposite. In that time myself and other members of the House, acting on the basis of the minister's original statements, gave out information which may well be inaccurate. This clearly interferes with the effective work of members of parliament.
If it is the case that the first statements were accurate and the second statements were false, then the minister is deliberately misrepresenting advice given him by the Department of Justice-I suspect, in order to bring pressure to bear on members of parliament to support and cause to pass quickly a piece of legislation they would otherwise oppose, the legislation
[Mr. Rodriguez.)
being Bill C-27 which contains certain amendments to which members are obviously opposed.
Mr. Speaker, either one or other of the statements of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) was misleading, and 1 believe deliberately so. In either case, my work as a member of parliament has been interfered with. If Your Honour should find that I have a question of privilege, I would move that the matter be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bud Cullen (Minister of Manpower and immigration):
subsubtopic: MR. RODRIGUEZ-UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-MINISTER'S STATEMENTS ON WITHHOLDING BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 welcome this opportunity to comment on the
April 19, 1977

question of privilege raised by the hon. member. On February 14 a press release was issued indicating that we did require legal authority in order to make the payments to those individuals who had not filed an appeal. It seemed to me, however, that given the decision made by Mr. Justice Addy affecting some 600 claimants, we should look into their claims, that we should compensate them without the need of appealing, and that we would be in a position to do the same with those who had gone ahead and had received their Quebec pension and their Canada pension. That was the information I received from the Department of Justice in the first instance.
The question has been raised in the House on a number of occasions and it has been raised in two ways. First, the leader of the Social Credit party raised the issue that members of my department or members of the Unemployment Insurance Commission had advised individuals that they would not be entitled to receive their unemployment insurance after January 1 in accordance with the legislation. That was the intention of the legislation. When those officials gave that information they were describing the bill as it was intended and as it was understood in this House. The question has been raised in the House on a number of occasions of whether the Unemployment Insurance Commission has the legal authority to make payment to claimants 65 years of age and over and claimants eligible for the dependency rate of benefit who were affected by Bill C-69.
More specifically, the question has been raised as to whether an amendment is required to the existing unemployment insurance legislation and/or to bill C-27 to make payments. I regret that some of the statements I have made on the subject may inadvertently have left an erroneous impression. I wish, therefore, to clarify the situation. The facts are as follows. First, the commission had the legal authority to make payments to the claimants who appealed. There were approximately 600. The amounts owing to these claimants have been determined and paid. Second, not being content with that and wishing to go the second mile and provide equity to those who had not filed an appeal but who had made application for the Quebec Pension Plan or the Canada Pension Plan, we sought, and received, iegal advice to the effect that an amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act was required to implement our decision to pay the claimants who did not appeal but who were in the same position as the appellants.
An amendment is contained in clause 48 of Bill C-27, to clarify the commission's powers to reconsider claims. It would be our intention to use the amended authority in Bill C-27 to make the payments to claimants who did not appeal, subject to final legal confirmation that the amended section can be applied retroactively. Therefore, we had to consult the Department of Justice on two questions of law. We needed to know this: Did we need an amendment? If so, was the amendment contained in the bill sufficient and would it apply retroactively? If it did not, redrafting of the amendment would be proposed to ensure its applicability to the claimants in question.
Privilege-Mr. Rodriguez
Third, in the meantime the commission contacted the individuals affected and reviewed their claims in an effort to ascertain the amounts which will be paid to those who qualify after clause 48 comes into force. In this connection 1 might mention that it would be our intent to implement this change as soon as possible after royal assent of Bill C-27 in order that payments could be effected expeditiously. Finally, the decision rendered by the umpire of the Federal Court is to the effect that our authority to pay claimants aged 65 and over is limited by the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act before they were amended by Bill C-69. This means that we only have legal authority to pay these claimants until such time as their Canada Pension Plan or Quebec Pension Plan becomes payable.
Considering the answers which have been given in the House-the hon. member suggested that there was a deliberate attempt to mislead, but I suggest it was not deliberate- and to make certain that he was getting the correct advice, I authorized my officials, without seeing the letter, to write to him and give him the correct picture which I have given him today. There was no intent to mislead, and if the hon. member was led to do some extracurricular work, I am sorry. The individuals involved have been contacted by the commission.

speechtext:
Order please. The hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) yesterday gave the Chair notice of his intention to raise a question of privilege, and yesterday indicated to the House that because of the minister's unavoidable absence he would prefer to hold the question over until today or when the minister could be present.
The preliminary question for the Chair always to decide is whether the motion or matter put forward by way of a proposed question of privilege is one which enjoys that special status which gives it precedence over any other matter before the House. If it has that special status, other business is set aside and the question put forward by the hon. member takes

precedence over other business of the House and must be considered by the House before it considers any other business.
The hon. member for Nickel Belt has certainly raised a serious grievance, obviously supported by the evidence he put forward in the House today. His debate on the matter was most persuasive. On the other hand, in order to find that the matter enjoys that special status of a question of privilege it seems to me that two conditions must be met. First, if the minister in fact misled the hon. member-and certainly other hon. members have given that indication-the Chair would have to find that the misleading by the minister was deliberate. The second condition is on somewhat weaker ground. It relates only to a question of the form of the motion of the hon. member. That is to say, the motion asks that the matter be referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. That, traditionally, has been held to be a form of motion too general to be accepted as a question of privilege because of the obvious problems of definition which would be put upon the shoulders of the committee if the motion were to succeed. I stress to hon. members of the House that I would not want to decide an important question of privilege on the basis only of the second ground, that is to say, on the basis of the form of the motion.
If, in fact, I thought that the matter were substantially correct and ought to have precedence over other matters, as questions of privilege certainly should have, I do not think I would allow a matter as important as that to fail on the grounds simply of form. However, I am more persuaded on the substantial ground, that is, whether the minister did in fact extend an apology to the member and other members who may have been misled by his answers. That is not the question for the Chair to decide. The question for the Chair to decide is whether, if the minister did, in fact, mislead members of the House, was his action in misleading members of the House of such a nature as to be a deliberate action and therefore one which affects the privileges of hon. members? If it was not a deliberate action on the part of the Minister, there are other remedies that lie in the hands of members.
If it is to be pursued by way of a question of privilege, I wish to stress again that in order to qualify as a question of privilege the Chair would have to find that not only had there been actions by the minister to mislead hon. members, but that those actions were calculated and deliberate by the minister for that purpose.
In the circumstances, the minister rose in his place. He explained the answers he had given. He indicated that if in fact hon. members were misled, that misleading was not a deliberate act on his part, but, in fact, was done in good faith on the strength of advice. Obviously, the Chair and the House must accept that explanation by the minister. Therefore, I cannot say, because I cannot find that any action on the part of the minister was deliberately calculated to mislead members, that the motion qualifies as a question of privilege within the definition as we know it.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (President of the Treasury Board):
subsubtopic: CONTINGENT LIABILITY FOR ALL FORMS OF INSURANCE

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the House adjourned this debate last night 1 was discussing the subject of anti-nuclear energy bias on the

part of the CBC. I want to quote in part a second letter that I received on this subject. The letter, dated October 29, 1976, was written by one of my constituents to the president of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation:
I am writing to you in connection with the broadcast of "Concern" on October 20, 1976. I refrained from writing earlier until I was able to obtain a transcript of the program.
As a hatchet job on an entire Canadian industry, it was very well done. As an objective discussion of a serious topic it was a disgrace to the CBC. Although there will presumably be equal time given for a rebuttal of this one-sided presentation, the public interest would have been better served by having knowledgeable people on the program, who could correct the untruths at the time, so that the listener could make an informed judgement between different points of view.
As just one example of an untruth, but one so simple as to demonstrate the low level of knowledge of the people participating in the program is the following statement by Mr. Ian Connerty (Canadian Coalition for Nuclear Responsibility).
$1.8 billion has been spent building a couple of reactors we do have in Canada and at this point in time today-the output of energy from those two reactors
is-
The writer goes on to say:
In fact, we have four large reactors operating at Pickering, Ontario. The first of these reactors went into service in 1971 and the fourth in 1973. The total cost of all four reactors was under $800 million, less than half the cost figure quoted by Mr. Connerty for two.
I should like to refer to a document entitled "The Canadian Nuclear Program: Safe and Sound" and commend its reading to members of the House. It is written by Mr. J. A. L. Robertson of the Chalk River Nuclear Laboratories, Atomic Energy of Canada. In it he discusses the issues involved in the use of nuclear energy, including reactor safety, radioactive releases, plutonium hazards and uranium supply, after which he offers some very useful conclusions. I feel this material should be read by anyone who intends to comment publicly on a very important Canadian industry in the energy field.
I should now like to say a few words, about freight rates. Section 276(1) of the Railway Act provides in part:
Except as otherwise provided by this act, all freight rates shall be compensatory.
This places a statutory duty upon the railways to ensure that all freight rates are compensatory except as otherwise provided by the Railway Act. The only exceptions to this provision are those set out in section 271 with respect to the Crowsnest pass rates and in section 272 with respect to eastern rates on grain and flour. Under the authority of this statute, the Canadian National Railways increased freight rates on wood material coming into a major veneer plant in Pembroke by 13.3 per cent early in 1976. This increase followed a previous increase of 15.38 per cent which was put into effect on January 1, 1975. In the course of a meeting in early February, 1977 between the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) and the maritime premiers, the topic of freight rates was discussed at great length. I quote from a news release dated February 8, 1977:
A topic of particular concern to the premiers was the impact on regional economic development of the application of cost effectiveness to the transportation system. Mr. Lang and the maritime premiers agreed that where economic development objectives required it those objectives would take precedence over the commercial viability of the services concerned.
April 19, 1977

During the discussion, Mr. Lang reiterated the federal government's commitment to regional economic development. To this end he emphasized that the objectives of a transportation system should be to serve as an effective instrument of support for the achievement of national and regional social and economic objectives as well as to achieve an efficient transportation system throughout Canada. Both Mr. Lang and his provincial colleagues have agreed that such a system should also provide accessibility and equity of treatment for users. Mr. Lang further indicated that following further consultation with the Atlantic provinces he would propose an amendment to Bill C-33 now before parliament to reflect that agreement.
I must congratulate the Minister of Transport on what he had to say with regard to the transportation needs of the maritime provinces, because he was dead right. In order to assist the natural resource-based industries in areas covered by the Regional Development Incentives Act, I would ask the Minister of Transport to take the same constructive and realistic approach to the question of freight rates in the Ottawa Valley when reviewing his suggested amendment to Bill C-33. Transportation costs are an important factor in attracting industry to areas which are not close to major markets. Such considerations are imperative when local raw materials have to be brought to a local industry. If freight rates are to be allowed to escalate on the basis of a provision in an unamended statute, such as section 276(1) of the Railway Act, this will only work against the excellent program which DREE is providing. Transportation and DREE should work together. I congratulate the minister for taking this particular initiative.
I should like to draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to a question which was asked in the House on February 8 by the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick). It appears in Hansard as follows:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion. Since the minister and his department have supposedly been in consultation with the province of Ontario about a joint venture, a general development agreement for the county of Renfrew since 1973, and promised in 1974 that Renfrew county would be in line for the next joint venture following the $17 million for Cornwall, and since in 1976 Ontario, because it could not get the co-operation and agreement of the federal government, had to do it alone and pump $2 million into Renfrew county, I ask the minister, when will the federal government honour its commitment and sign an agreement with the province of Ontario to help with infrastructure and other basic developments needed in this high unemployment county?
This is a real concern of ours. The fact is that nowhere in the records of that Cornwall meeting did the Hon. Mr. White, who was representing the Ontario government, or the minister responsible for DREE, ever mention Renfrew county.
Joint federal-provincial studies are currently under way regarding the development of a potential GDA initiative involving the Renfrew-Pembroke area. Discussions originally started in 1974 were delayed until recently to await completion of provincial development strategy for Renfrew county. Therefore, it is not the fault of the federal government that this matter has been delayed. In the meantime, recognizing the area's special needs, on the expiration of the special area program for Renfrew county on December 31, 1975, the federal government responded by including the Pembroke-Renfrew area as part of the designated region for Ontario under the Regional Development Incentives Act. This designa-
The Budget-Mr. Hopkins
tion will extend until 1981 and I am grateful to the minister for making this possible.
Since the special area designation in April, 1970, incentive offers totalling $9,927,959 have been made to companies locating or expanding in the Renfrew-Pembroke area. The precise provincial government outlays included in the $2 million referred to in the question by the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton do not involve the general development agreement in any way and would not qualify for inclusion because of prior commitments by the province. So the way that question was worded was misleading.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with a good deal of attention to the last speaker, the hon. member for Renfrew North-Nipissing East (Mr. Hopkins). At one time he was a protege of mine and I often wondered why he went astray or had got off the beaten path over the years. I listened very carefully to what he had to say, because he is a likeable fellow. Then all at once it struck me: having been taught under Professor Lower at Queen's University, how could he do anything else?
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) is, as always, in for a good deal of criticism, as most finance ministers are, though some point praise. But he is confronted with a difficult problem in trying to bring out a satisfactory budget. After 14 years of Liberal governments spending beyond their means, it is no wonder we are in deep trouble today. Some may say that that is pretty partisan, but I want to quote the Prime Minister, (Mr. Trudeau).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No one would ever say that of you.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Thank you very much. The Prime Minister said in Toronto that we were spending more than we earned, that the other fellow we are trading with spends less than he earns and produces more. He should have added that he was the fellow who, with his government, printed the money that led us down this path. I should like to deal with a little bit of history for a few moments by reading an excerpt from the monthly letter published by the Royal Bank of Canada:
What is the purpose of all our office work from the clay tablets of Babylon to the punched tape of today's electronic machines except to provide the history of transactions?
There is one qualification to be made: we must use only what is true, significant, and applicable. We must, as Jean Jaur&s, French statesman, philosopher and orator said: "take from the altars of the past the fire-not the ashes."
Keeping that in mind, let me go back to when the electors of this country handed over the reins of power to the Liberals in 1963. At that time Canada was a prosperous country, having the second highest standard of living in the world and an inflation rate of 2 per cent. We had a trade surplus for the first time in ten years, unemployment had been checked, and industrial competition and productivity had been brought to

new heights because of tax laws which encouraged the supplementing of outdated and outmoded methods with new machinery and equipment. Vocational and technical schools had been built all across the country by the federal government to train the people required to operate this new machinery. We had industrial expansion and growth, as a result of which it became necessary to bring in increased numbers of immigrants.
This was the picture in the Diefenbaker era. The revaluation of the dollar gave us a realistic tool with which to encourage industrial expansion and more manufacturing of our own raw resources, in addition to encouraging exports and discouraging imports, all of which prompted economists of the day to state that Canada was one of the best managed countries in the world. Our world markets were enlarged through our going out and doing a hard selling job.
The minister of trade and commerce, the minister of finance and the prime minister himself travelled to many countries. I had the good fortune to be with the then prime minister, Mr. Diefenbaker, on one of those trips and saw first-hand his approach. Every Canadian embassy was aware that the cocktail route would not take care of all our problems. There was fierce competition in the marketplace. The Marshall plan was providing Germany and Japan with new machinery and new equipment; technology in the United States was at work. We had to meet that competition. Any Canadian embassy that did not make its government aware of what its host nation needed and what could be sold to it was warned that promotions had to be on realities. They had to have the staff, and they had to have the personnel who not only looked after the niceties of diplomacy and diplomatic relations but also the realities of the necessity to trade and to sell Canadian goods in the markets of the world. In other words, they were to earn their salaries which had to be paid by the people back home.
In London, George Drew at that time was the High Commissioner to Great Britain. He did an excellent job. Now my old friend, Paul Martin, the present High Commissioner to Great Britain, is working as hard as the traditional beaver doing the same.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Paul always earned his salary. When he was in opposition-I sat on the other side of the House then-he was "Dennis the Menace". Good luck to him, and may he long remain in his present position.
As a result of all this, wheat sales were opened up and trade was encouraged, particularly in food supplies. Wheat was sold to countries such as China and Japan. I happened to be in Japan with the prime minister when I saw the children there in the high schools and public schools eating white bread sandwiches and drinking milk. Traditionally, of course, they were eating rice before this. That was salesmanship. We owe a great debt of thanks to General McArthur who was there and put in charge of that country after the last war. That was obtaining
April 19, 1977

new markets and our government of John Diefenbaker took advantage of them. As a result of all this, our wheat sales rose to $1 billion.
I could go on and on. Who would not long for those good old days? There were no divisions in Canada under prime minister St. Laurent and prime minister Diefenbaker. People were Canadians. Why? Because everyone was treated justly. There was no need, then, for saying that the land was strong. We were strong. There was no need to call for a just society. It was not until we had a few years of Liberal government that we needed the just society. And what a just society! Benson's "folly" passed rules and regulations in tax reform, pushed through parliament by closure, which half the members of parliament never had a chance to read. If they did read them, they did not understand them. Half the accountants in the country still cannot interpret them.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Just a few remarks?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Do not blame altogether the Ministers of Finance. John Turner could not make them work, and he resigned in disgust when changes he wanted were not backed up by his cabinet colleagues. After all, freedom of movement in this government is becoming financially narrower. As a matter of fact, before leaving the past, it might be well to remind us all that in 1964, really the last year of the legacy left from a previously well-run economy, total federal government spending was less than $7.2 billion. The expected deficit alone for this year is around $7.5 billion, on which there is interest which the Canadian people have to pay of around $500 million. This will add to every taxpayer's bill.
It is a bit unfair for us to compare the increase in Canadian labour costs with those of the United States without presenting the facts. I feel strongly about this. The Canadian taxpayer, if everything is taken into account, pays about double the tax that his American counterpart pays. If the tax breaks had been anything of significance, labour demands would have been much less insistent and our goods would have been priced a little lower. Indeed, the government itself sets the worst example for labour, industry and the Canadian taxpayer in general. From 1970 to 1976 the government increased its spending 150 per cent.
If you look at this another way, you will see right away that this took about 8 per cent of the gross national product. It is a sad fact that the government takes from the Canadian people about one-fifth of their income. While all of this is going on, the labour force in the last ten years in industry and manufacturing fell from 40 per cent to 20 per cent. This is one thing that makes you very sick. It was cut in half. Manufacturing is the lifeblood of labour employment and sales abroad. In addition to all of this, with unemployment at an all-time high, our growth rate is slower and inflation remains high. Our deficit runs higher than the United States, Great Britain, Germany, Japan and Italy.
Here we are, in Canada, with tremendous natural resources. No country in the world is as blessed with natural resources per capita as we are. In Japan there is no unemployment, yet
The Budget-Mr. Rynard
most of its food and raw resources must be brought in from abroad. For example, Japan is able to buy raw resources here in Canada and ship them back to us as manufactured articles for sale in Canada. Our trade deficit, with 23 million people, is $4.3 billion. Great Britain, whose raw resources are in very limited supply, most of them having to be imported also, had a trade deficit of only $3.3 billion. Canada has the worst record of any industrial country in the world.
While all of this was happening, our service industries over the same period of time that manufacturing was declining by nearly half went up by 6 per cent. Seven per cent of our work force is now employed in government administration. We spend more money, or more of our gross national product, than any industrial nation in the world. The figures startle you when you consider that 25 per cent of every dollar earned must come from our exports. When I refer to the service industries, that is something we spend among ourselves. As the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) said, it is like taking in the other guy's washing.
Small industries such as Shakespeare in Orillia must purchase some parts of their raw materials for their manufactured articles. On this raw material they must also pay a 15 per cent customs duty. A so-called underdeveloped nation has no duty to pay on its finished products. I refer to a new factory, and this is what happened. A newspaper article in the Packet and Times, Orillia, reads as follows:
Shakespeare Co. Ltd., of Orillia, which makes fishing rods and reels, as well as gun cases, will close its manufacturing operation here on April 15, putting an estimated 30 people out of work. Bill Ardell, the company's vice-president and general manager said today.
This situation is primarily a result of our inability to compete with imported fishing goods from Korea, Taiwan, and Japan, which are not charged any import duties by the Canadian government-
The hon. member who just finished speaking before me has left the House. He said that we are going to help small business. How are you helping small business? I am talking about small business right now. What are you doing for it? The article continues:
The vice-president noted his company has to pay a 15 per cent duty on raw materials . . .
Fourteen employees will be retained to staff the administrative, sales, service and warehousing departments-
They will bring in the goods from outside this country, giving jobs to other countries. The underdeveloped country has no tax to pay even though they buy the same raw product right from the United States. This is how we are treating labour and small business. The article continues:
The minimum starting wage of Shakespeare's plant employees is $3.30 an hour, and increases are given on an incentive basis . ..
The workers were notified recently that their jobs would end ...
The Orillia plant is Shakespeare's only Canadian manufacturing outlet, and the company's American head office is located in Columbia, South Carolina ...
The decision to close manufacturing operations in Orillia was arrived at here; the final agreement was made with the American company.
They could not meet that type of competition. We cannot remain competitive on the Canadian market. Some of the
80012 -24j/2

April 19, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Rynard
companies that compete with us pay their employees less than $900 a year, which is what we pay our workers for six weeks of work. Also, those companies have no duty to pay. I hope the Minister of State for Small Business (Mr. Marchand) will keep this in mind, because nothing was done to help that company even though its situation was well advertised-and 1 have three pages of it. 1 could refer to other companies in Simcoe North and recount what has happened to them; how they have had to bring in parts from other countries and put them together here because they could not meet competition. The reason is that we have priced ourselves out of world markets. Many small industries in my constituency face the same problem due to the rising cost of energy.
The government has no energy policy. There is little worthwhile research carried out on the development of new sources of energy from methane gas, wind and sun augmented by gas or electricity when necessary. Just last night President Carter of the United States gave a warning that if that country is to survive economically, Americans will have to conserve the energy they are using and find new sources.
It was interesting to hear him speak of coal in his speech. Few countries in the world have the coal supplies which are found in Canada and in the United States. What are we doing to develop coal? I wonder what the Minister of Finance thinks about his side-kick, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie), telling him that all will be well by 1990. I am sorry the minister is not in the House at present. The minister of energy of Ontario has stated that Ontario will be importing two million barrels of oil a day. As I have said, President Carter says that we have underestimated the world's supply of oil and gas. We must get together with them and see what the true story is on Mr. Carter's words that we will certainly be short of supplies. We will be going downhill economically unless we cut down on our consumption of energy and find new sources of it.
The richest country in the world today in natural resources, per capita, is in deep trouble. In the 1950s and 1960s the gross national product grew by 2 per cent a year. Now it is only growing by 1 per cent. Why is that? A program to keep in balance, wages, salaries and other related factors should be growing at the same rate as the GNP. One does not have to be a mathematician to realize that at 2 per cent per year, if you start to work when you are young you could double your money in 35 years. You would have an incentive to work. However, at 1 per cent per year it would take 70 years to double your money. There would be no incentive to work, and without it one loses one's drive. There is nothing to look forward to; your only hope lies in winning a Wintario or a Loto Canada lottery. It is a real tragedy when there is no incentive to work. Perhaps that is why we are less productive than the United States. We are really going back to the times when the pioneer farmer worked all his life just to make things a little easier for his family. He worked from dawn till dark without hope of making money for his old days.
A government politically geared to attracting votes is giving us more than we can afford. The present government could

never forecast costs. It is, itself, the spender. We needed more and more money and the printing machines turned it out. The costs of our manufactured goods increase, and we must have more money in order to buy them. This puts the costs of the products up, so we cannot meet competition abroad. Actually, we cannot even meet it in our own domestic markets. We have had to borrow more and more money abroad just to keep us afloat. Now we are paying out over $11 billion more in interest and dividends than we are receiving.
Basic pay rates should be increased only as production and profits increase. This gives incentives to labour. I am sure that few firms would refuse to discuss their financial statements with labour. This would increase worker interest in the success of the company and in the part they are playing to achieve it. It should be possible for the government to establish new industries in areas where the companies themselves might not be able to do so by building roads, instituting housing programs and building new sites. In 1958 the government built "roads to resources". The provincial premiers played a certain part in that. Some of them have told me that never at any time in the history of this country was there a program as successful as "roads to resources" which was started under the Diefen-baker government. As a matter of fact, it is the only time in Canadian history that a railroad was built which paid dividends. 1 am referring to the Pine Point railway which carried goods and supplies to the Pacific coast.
If 100,000 jobs were produced through a program, this would add about $1 billion to the economy. Of the million or so unemployed, how many are physically, mentally or emotionally disabled and should be retired on a pension? There are a good many. A gentleman came to see me the other day, a war veteran who after the war was over went to work in construction. He is an engineer. He was hurt and received a pension from the Ontario Workmen's Compensation board. Finally he took a lump sum because he wanted to return to work, and he went to work for the federal government, of all things. This man has a bad back; he has to wear a brace all the time. He suffers from numbness in both legs and he is in pain. A year and a half ago he fell and hurt himself again, requiring surgery. He is totally disabled, yet the government is not willing to settle his claim. I saw him the other day, and I will fight his case because I believe an injustice is being done to a man who cannot sit for 10 or 15 minutes, who is taking pills all the time, who can only walk with a cane. Asking that man to work is inhumane and unsafe for the employer.
I wonder how many such cases there are in this country, and I wonder why my friend, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has not spoken up for them as he has for other forgotten cases. I would say that probably one in 50 people cannot be employed because of one type of disability or another. There are probably 50,000 people who should be receiving disability pensions instead of unemployment insurance benefits or welfare when they run out. Each year we import migrant workers to harvest our fruit, vegetable and tobacco crops. Yet it has been estimated that in spite of this extra migrant labour there have been losses amounting to $200
April 19, 1977

million to $300 million because growers have not been able to obtain labour. Why do we have to import foreign labour? We have a society that will not do its own cleaning up. Why do we have to pay through the nose for it? What is the total cost of transportation and housing for these 5,000 or more migrant workers who are brought in?
There are many people who want light jobs or are new to the job, and they could be used if the minimum wage rate was lower and paid according to the work they want to do. We have to be competitive and our minimum wage scales must be on a par with those with whom we have to compete. I was told recently by an agricultural expert that we pay 30 cents to 60 cents an hour more for 20 per cent less production than the Americans pay right across the border at Niagara. It is no wonder that they can sell their Del-Monte peaches in our marketplaces. We must compete and have lower taxes and less government spending, or we will go down in history as the most profligate nation of all time. I am not blaming labour for all this, because when a government takes one-fifth of what people earn they do not have very much left after living. I would hazard a guess that we would save about $2 billion if the cases mentioned earlier were well administered, and job-creation properly researched to provide jobs that lead to more jobs which need to be carried out. We also had a deficit in tourism of well over $1 billion. That meant we spent well over $1 billion more than visitors spent in Canada. That is $1 billion, in spite of the Olympics on which we sunk another $500 million.
We need the imagination of a government like the one we had back in the Diefenbaker days when we could make this country attractive and when people came here to visit. We need the imagination of the Tory government of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) of 1957 to 1963 which had everyone coming my way to hit the Yukon trail and relive the days of the Klondike gold rush. The old girls were not there, but the new ones took their place and to the ribald songs of 1898 the saga was replayed. If my memory serves me correctly, we had an excellent surplus in the tourist trade that year.

speechtext: I question the necessity of fact-finding tours with committees being sent hither and thither. You would not be found crabbing around the Prime Minister if you were out of the country testing the waters of the Mediterranean. Perhaps that is the reason he wants to get rid of some of those people. I know some hon. members on both sides go on these trips. But are they all necessary? We have energy problems galore, and we are sending committees out on fact-finding tours studying energy. 1 say that the people back home, manufacturers and labour, are finding it too tough for the government to be lending millions of dollars to Castro in Cuba at low interest rates when he at the same time is sending an army to Angola. subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
These housekeeping items probably cost another $1 billion, and I have already taken $3 billion off our deficit of $7.5 billion. We are simply not producing enough to afford even our present standard of living. We have fallen a long way since 1945. We then ranked number five among producing nations, and we had the second highest standard of living. Neither a strong land nor a just society has stopped the skid. How are we to get out of this mess without irreparable harm being done to this country?
Let us unite Canada. Never before in history has it been as divided as it is today. We are antagonized by unilingualism, bilingualism, multilingualism, and so forth, and our economy is in difficulty. Bilingualism has cost billions of dollars, but what has it really done to unite, or has it disunited? That is what we must ask ourselves. I was brought up in an English community. When I went to school, four languages were offered and two of them were compulsory. I studied all four- English, French, Latin and German. I passed in Latin, the grammar, virgil and written. I was able to pass my French grammar and French literature with fairly good marks. I passed German, but in English I was only ordinary. I was not forced to study those languages. I liked studying French.

April 19, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Broadbent
I think what the Prime Minister stated last night in Winnipeg got nearer to what we should really be doing. We should give people a chance to learn a second language-but let us not force language down their throats, because we will only antagonize them and drive them into multi-separatism.
Let us cut waste, whether it be waste of electricity, gas, oil, coal, wood or any energy-producing material. Let us increase incentives and write-offs to industry because it is labour-intensive and will, hopefully, produce manufactured articles which can be sold in world markets and also increase the hiring of labour as production is stepped up. Let us stop living beyond our means. Our neighbours are living cheaper and producing more. Let us stop government spending and the printing of more and more money. Then, and only then, can we return to challenge the world as we should.
We all love Canada and we all want to be Canadians. I am proud to be a Canadian. The people on my father's side originally came from Europe, to Ireland and to Canada. I have French relatives and I am proud of that. Let us pull up our socks and get to work. Back in the forties we showed the world that there was no nation which could outdo us in the fields of production and ingenuity-on an equal basis. God knows, we have more raw resources than any country in the world. In that respect we are rich. In closing I would like to leave this little verse with the House:
The heights achieved by great men reached and kept were not attained by sudden flight. But they, while their companions slept, were toiling upward in the night.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all last week the hard working, industrious flacks in the office of the Prime Minister were busy selling what was described as "A speech of major significance"-the performance of which many people witnessed on television last night. The working staff in the Prime Minister's office did this with all the enthusiasm well paid officials can muster under such circumstances. Wherever they were gathered, Canadians were urged to huddle in deep and eager anticipation before their television sets to hear the latest words of advice-indeed, of wisdom-on the question of national unity. It was, we were assured, to be a grand performance. Canadians should assess that speech last night in light of the budget that is now before the House and in light of the performance of this government since 1968. I say this because in life in general, and in politics in particular, it is performance-not talk-that counts.
For me last night's speech had two important aspects. First, in its discussion of bilingualism it was a speech that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) should surely have made in Canada- whether in the west, in the east or in southern Ontario-not last night, not in the middle of April, 1977, but in the middle of April, 1969 or 1970. In short, Mr. Speaker, the speech was some seven or eight years late. Bilingualism as advocated, explained and implemented by this government has failed to gain acceptance in large measure because its principal advocate, the Prime Minister, has failed to translate the meaning of

that policy and program to Canadians as one of language equality. His failure on this issue is that serious.
What the Prime Minister had to say about the Official Languages Act last night all members of my party and, indeed, I think most civilized Canadians wherever they live would agree with. What he said is involved in the principle of the Official Languages Act is not special or privileged treatment for any group in Canada, but equality of rights for our two principal cultures, French-speaking and English-speaking. In that the Prime Minister is correct. In that, the New Democratic Party supports him. I repeat, in getting around to explaining that important principle of the Official Languages Act just last night, he is seven or eight years late.
It is important to note that this policy of the Prime Minister-which is almost his only policy in terms of holding the country together-certainly was his only policy in 1968 and has remained so since. In terms of his public utterances, it is important to note that not once since 1968 has the Prime Minister gone across the country to try to explain in ordinary language, to ordinary people, what that policy is all about. For him to suggest, as he did last night, that somehow Canadians were failing to respond appropriately to a policy they did not understand is surely the height of irresponsibility. It has been his responsibility in the past seven or eight years to explain that what was at stake was language equality. In that he has been a colossal failure.
Apart from the discussion of the Official Languages Act and what it revealed about the government's failure, the most significant aspect of last night's speech was its total failure, as an allegedly serious speech, to indicate even one positive initiative the government would attempt in coming to grips with a myriad of economic problems that Canadians face, whether they live in Atlantic Canada, Quebec, Ontario or, given the location of the speech, in the west. Not one new, detailed principle was presented by the Prime Minister.
Like the budget before us now, the Prime Minister's speech last night totally ignored the economic realities which are at the root of so many of the problems faced by our people wherever they may live. The rhetoric was fine, but after analysis substance was found to be totally lacking. I did not have an opportunity to watch the Prime Minister on television or listen to him on radio last night.

I say to the Liberal backbencher that I am going to devote a good part of my comments to what the Prime Minister had to say, because I read the speech with care. It is
April 19, 1977

substance that matters, and too often with radio or television the substance is missed.
It is rare that we have the opportunity of hearing the Prime Minister in this House. On occasion he deigns to come in and drop a few bons mots and pass through after that. In this instance he made a speech outside the House, but so that it will be on the record somewhere I should like to quote some of his words. Here is what the Prime Minister said:
Perhaps the first danger would be to underestimate the seriousness of the situation in Quebec, the determination of the Parti Quebecois government. Paradoxically, because the Quebec situation is so serious, Canadians and their federal government cannot afford to become morbidly preoccupied with separatism, dealing with that situation alone.
He went on to say:
On the contrary. The separatist danger in Quebec requires us, in fact, to continue working as hard as possible to reduce unemployment and improve the economy; to provide better management in government; to meet the aspirations of western Canadians; to do many things.
That is very well said, indeed. He continued-and Liberal members will be pleased to hear the following words:
There are two important reasons for this. First, if Quebeckers in their referendum are to choose to live in Canada, it will have to be a Canada they want to live in-
That is very profound.
-which depends in part on a whole range of national policies and programs. Second, unless all Canadians are reasonably happy with their lot, problems of national unity may erupt again and again in region after region.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What is wrong with that?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Nothing is wrong with that. As a statement of purpose, it is a quote I can support and I am sure all members of my party, and indeed most Canadians, can support it. But the fact is that one of the general characteristics of platitudes is that most people believe them. But it is an utterance that the Prime Minister, of all people, should have choked on. It is a statement which inadvertently outlines the government's own failure. Coming from the Prime Minister, I say it is hypocritical. Those are the words of a man who has failed Canadians in the past and who has done nothing since November 15 to change their future for the better. The Prime Minister has decided to save Canada-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Platitudes!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I say to the hon. member from my neighbouring constituency that I will deal with the substance in a moment. The Prime Minister has decided to save Canada by substituting platitudes for action. Unfortunately for television viewers, they are in for a series of television reruns, reducing the debate on our country's future to the level of late night television trivia-sombre platitudes totally unsupported by action.
Let us consider the second sentence in the above quotation. I should like to quote it again, particularly for Liberal backbenchers who do not spend a lot of time reading. The Prime Minister said:
The Budget-Mr. Broadbent
Paradoxically, because the Quebec situation is so serious, Canadians and their federal government cannot afford to become morbidly preoccupied with separatism, dealing with that situation alone.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, "morbidly preoccupied with separatism" is an accurate description of the state of mind of the Prime Minister and his government. They are morbidly preoccupied and in a state of total inaction. Instead, they should be positively revealing, through action, the values of a national government committed to economic justice, opportunity and reform. Surely Quebeckers want that. Surely that is why they elected the present provincial government on November 15. Surely, also, that is what Canadians elsewhere want. They are tired of talk and platitudes. They want action-but they are not getting it from the Prime Minister.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They are not getting it from the Liberals; of that you can be sure.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Prime Minister made the following assertion, as he continued his speech, and surely even he ought to have choked while uttering these words:
The separatist danger in Quebec requires us to continue working as hard as possible to reduce unemployment and improve the economy.
Yes, he said we must continue working as hard as possible to reduce unemployment and improve the economy. Mr. Speaker, he neither choked nor smiled when he uttered those words.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He should have croaked.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is absurd to suggest that the government has worked in the recent past to deal with unemployment. And it is cruel nonsense to imply, as he did, that the government is doing anything about future unemployment. As members of the government party acknowledge in private, and as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) has sometimes said publicly in moments of candour, the budget we are now debating assumes tacitly that throughout 1977 more than one million Canadians will remain unemployed. The government callously has accepted the continuance this year of the highest level of unemployment since the "great depression". The government, in short, has coldly decided not to deal at all with unemployment. It has refused to recognize that when more than one million Canadians are without jobs, more than
300,000	of them being in Quebec, those very people and the several million affected by their hapless state are questioning not only national unity but the very foundations of the society in which we live.
The Prime Minister concluded the statement I quoted by suggesting that unless all Canadians remain happy with their lot, "problems of national unity may erupt again and again in region after region".

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
After hearing the Prime Minister's television address last night and comparing what he said with the

contents of the budget, some Canadians, perhaps in their naivety, might ask themselves if the Prime Minister has read the budget. Does the Prime Minister know what is really going on? Members of this House know very well that the Prime Minister knows what is going on and knows what is in the budget. All Canadians should realize that the Prime Minister's statement last night on television, like his statements in 1968, 1972 and 1974, had everything to do with rhetoric and nothing to do with reality or commitment. The Prime Minister is a master dilettante with power.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Right on.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He is a man committed to doing nothing except maintaining his and his party's political power.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Nonsense. We have one of the best Prime Ministers in the world.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Perhaps his most cynical utterance last night concerns his new-found sympathies for western Canadians. I am sure all people west of the Lakehead and east of the Rockies were moved by the Prime Minister's touching sympathy for western Canadians.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Especially Jack Horner.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He said, as I am told by those who watched his television address, without smiling that he was not ashamed of the progress made in the west ever since the western economic opportunities conference of July, 1973. That statement itself was shameless. He certainly was not ashamed of it, although he ought to have been. The Prime Minister neglected to mention that the conference of July, 1973, was called when the government was in a minority position in the House of Commons. The truth is that the Liberals had to forget ideas going back almost to the time of Genghis Khan and respond to some of the genuine concerns of western Canada where the NDP then formed three of the four provincial governments.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

They finally discovered that they should have a meeting in western Canada and that they could sit down and discuss policies.
