April 19, 1977

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, as the hon. lady says, "Wow!" What did the Prime Minister say at that conference? What were his immortal closing words at the conference?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Read them.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He said:
Well, thus ends the one and only western economic opportunities conference.
What the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) should have added was, "So, too, ended the Liberal government's commitment to pursue seriously the mutually agreed upon western objectives". Virtually nothing of benefit to the west has followed the conference. And much that has been harmful to Canadians in that part of our country that was already on the law books has remained. There has been total inaction by the government in terms of western concern since that conference. Moving the Mint one day to Winnipeg and another day taking Air Canada and moving it elsewhere hardly constitutes a contribution to what the Prime Minister described as a need for economic opportunities in the west. Nor does supporting multinational companies in the courts in their battle against the people of the province of Saskatchewan help western Canadians.
In three areas of direct policy concern brought up at that conference to which the Prime Minister alluded there has been nothing short of total failure by the Prime Minister and his government to live up to commitments that were made. Just consider them. In transportation we have increased foot-dragging, bungling and, worst of all, the emergence of Otto Lang as Minister of Transport. A communique issued by the premiers who met in western Canada last year to discuss their regions stated:
The western premiers rejected the user-pay philosophy advocated by the federal goverment and expressed dismay at the definite reversal of policy commitments given at the WEOC conference held in Calgary in July of 1973 and by the hon. Jean Marchand.
They said a year ago that the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) turned upside down the commitments made by his predecessor, commitments made at a conference to which the Prime Minister referred with pride last night. The present minister has, in the form of Bill C-33, presented legislation to this House which has the user-pay philosophy as its principal theoretical concept. The premiers of western Canada rightly rejected the user-pay philosophy at the WEOC conference. The Prime Minister had then agreed with the rejection. The previous minister of transport rejected it. The present Minister of Transport, however, is bringing it in in this bill.
Today in the House I asked the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) if the government was going to follow up in some way the general commitment made last night over television, and would it do so by indicating it is going to withdraw that bill from the House until it can be discussed with the provincial ministers involved? I got a negative answer to this specific request to give some flesh to the platitudinous in the commitment to the west made yesterday by the Prime Minister.
The Budget-Mr. Broadbent
Another quote from the western premiers conference of last year reads as follows:
They agreed that progress relative to increased responsiveness from federal transportation policy has been disappointingly slow. Moreover, concern was expressed that the present federal Minister of Transportation, the hon. Otto Lang, has not lived up to definitive commitment given by the former minister, Mr. Marchand, in February, 1975, to correcting a number of serious inequities affecting western transportation.
Following the speech made by the Prime Minister last night,
I also rose in the House today to ask if we were going to get some shift in attitude on this. I pointed out that the freight rates as they now exist discriminate against the prairie rape-seed-crushing industry. This is something that westerners have known for many years, took for granted and now have protested.
A good illustration of the willingness of the Prime Minister and the government to do something for the west would be to change the discriminatory freight rate structure as it affects this industry which is vital to western Canadians. The answer I got from the Acting Prime Minister today, within 12 hours of the Prime Minister's speech, is that the government has no intention of reversing this discriminatory policy.
Only a few days ago Canadian National Railways refused to consider improving the roadbed of the Hudson Bay rail line so that it could carry Canadian government hopper cars and thus move more quickly and efficiently western grain to the port of Churchill. That is a request that western premiers of all political parties have made for many years, to improve facilities at the port of Churchill in order to transport grain produced by Canadian farmers. And, again, it has been turned down in terms of concrete action by the present government.
The litany of transport policy failures in particular areas is only made worse by the government when one considers that in terms of general transportation policy we are virtually in a non-existent state. Instead of imaginative, concrete, specific innovations that would improve transportation policy, we get the Prime Minister going on television and simply adding hypocrisy to an unfortunate situation.
The second area of western concern talked about by western premiers at their conference last year and totally ignored by the present government concerns banking policy. For many years western provinces, regardless of their government, have expressed their concern that the Bank Act be changed to give greater western input in determining their own financial priorities. What do we get from this government? We get a white paper on the Bank Act that is going to give more, not less, power to the federal government. It is going to impinge on the existing right of the provincial governments to have legislative authority over caisses populaires in Quebec and credit unions in the other provinces.
Opposition to the Bank Act change proposed by the federal government has come principally from western Canada where credit unions play a major role for the ordinary people. As recently as this afternoon in the House of Commons, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) indicated there would be no change on the part of the government's plans.

April 19, 1977
The Budget-Hon. J.-P. Guay
A third area of concern to western Canadians has been the development of their resources. Last night the Prime Minister made reference, again without irony, I take it, to his commitment to resource development in western Canada. I wondered why the Prime Minister did not choke when he uttered his words about the Liberal government's concern for western resource development in western Canada. He knows it was his government that took the unprecedented step of opposing the province of Saskatchewan in court in defence of multinational corporations in their battle with the government of Saskatchewan which was taking concrete action to get greater control over their own resources for the people of that province. Instead of lining up with and defending the people of that province in their determination to have greater control, the national Liberals lined up with their friends the multinational corporations.
Mir. Deputy Speaker: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member, but his allotted time has expired. He may continue only with unanimous consent. Does the hon. member have consent?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Agreed.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank hon. members for their indulgence. I will conclude very quickly with the following observation. The general point I have been making in my speech with regard to the Prime Minister's efforts over television last night is as follows. The government has with regard to western Canada, the same attitude as it has for Canadians elsewhere-no commitment. It has no general philosophy which says that the principal task of a government is to be concerned with the real problems of ordinary people, and that following up this general commitment there is an obligation on a government to bring down policies which will implement it.
There is nothing in the Prime Minister's attitude to suggest he has that kind of commitment. Instead, we have the opposite. Just as in 1968, 1972 and 1974 we had election slogans and campaigns which were totally devoid of substance, so now we have at this most serious period in our national history, a Prime Minister who almost six months after the election of a separatist government in Quebec goes on television uttering the most banal platitudes, a Prime Minister who has not introduced one new idea, one single policy proposal to deal with the ordinary problems of Canadians whether in the east, in the centre, or in the west. I say, on behalf of my hon. friends, that this is not the route to building a strong, independent, united country. It is not the route we require of a prime minister who has a commitment to make to the country. It is the route solely of a dilettante.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have this opportunity to present some of my views on the budget. Let me begin by outlining the major considerations which concerned the government in drafting this document. The government faced the prospect of having to stimulate the economy in order to provide jobs for

the fastest growing work force in the western world without setting off inflation again. None of the members of this House like to see unemployment such as we face today; neither do any of us wish a return to runaway inflation. These two considerations limited the government's options in preparing the budget.
It has been called a cautious budget, and rightly so. Inflation is still a serious problem despite controls, and unemployment is far higher than any Canadian would like to see. In these circumstances the government rightly felt the need to be cautious. This was no time to experiment with the economic health of the nation merely to suit a number of critics who are concerned with their own narrow interests, either personal or political.
The third major concern of the government was the level of its own spending. The government had no wish to refuel inflation with its own budget deficit. Along with our general concern about inflation and unemployment, this made it necessary to limit our deficit and, more important still, made it necessary to spend those deficit dollars on the best possible mix of programs to create jobs without starting another round of inflation.
The government was therefore concerned with finding the proper balance. And it is, of necessity, a cautious balance between three major and conflicting areas of concern; first, the level of government spending; second, inflation, and third unemployment. Since the government's own spending always has the potential of causing renewed inflation, it was directed, wisely I think, toward longer term stimulation of the economy. The investment incentives directed toward business will move through the economy more slowly than other measures might have done, but certainly much more safely.
Much of the government deficit arises from efforts directed at minimizing the effects of unemployment, especially among young Canadians. Almost half a billion dollars is going into Canada Works and Young Canada Works programs alone.
The government has also directed attention to lowering the tax burden borne by low and middle income Canadians. The automatic tax relief granted by the indexation of the basic personal exemption alone will put $900 million into the hands of Canadians. Critics of the budget conveniently forget the magnitude of this program which compensates Canadians for the loss of purchasing power due to inflation. We have also raised the exemption for dependent children by $50 per child. Again, this puts a healthy amount into the pockets of low income Canadians with children. The government also raised the employment expense deduction by 66 per cent, from $150 to $250. All these plans taken together will put substantial amounts into the hands of Canadians so they can decide where best to spend or invest. The money will also serve to increase their spending power and, in the longer term, to increase demand in a variety of industries without leading to another round of inflation.
The government has also made certain fiscal adjustments to encourage business to expand across Canada. The government went one step further here by recognizing that certain areas or
April 19, 1977

regions need more stimulation than others. Thus, the government has introduced varying rates of investment tax credit in different regions of Canada; for example, 10 per cent in the maritimes, 10.5 per cent in Manitoba, and 5 per cent nationally. The government has also altered the investment climate for average Canadians through a variety of measures such as allowing capital gains on Canadian stocks to be included in the $1,000 interest and dividend deduction. This will serve to encourage the participation of small investors in the economy and provide a little more incentive toward taking risk in Canadian stocks.
I should like now to read from a statement issued by S. F. Hughes, executive director of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce concerning the budget proposals:
The federal budget announced by finance minister Donald Macdonald was based on an accurate assessment of the difficult dilemma facing Canada today, that is, the need to provide some stimulus to the economy while avoiding a resurgence of inflationary forces and an increase in the federal cash deficit.
The Chamber regards the budget as moderately expansionary in nature. The announced restraints in federal spending will be more than offset by the effect of the tax reductions and will result in a significant yet manageable growth in the government's deficit. However, anything more in terms of deficit would have been irresponsible.
Almost one half of the tax incentives announced in the budget will benefit individual Canadians either as wage earners or as investors.
We support Mr. Macdonald's proposal to phase out controls rather than end them abruptly. This approach is in keeping with the Chamber's perception of the most equitable way of removing the controls.
As I said earlier, this is a cautious budget. I have explained the economic reasons underlying this caution and I have drawn attention to some of the measures we were able to introduce to stimulate the economy despite these limits.
Now I should like to go into some of the social or, if you like, political reasons for which the government had to be cautious. We are still waiting from some agreement from labour and business with respect to the need for restraint in their demands. All of us are concerned about the behaviour of these two powerful groups in the economy when price and wage controls are removed. Unemployment in Canada is high, as I have already said, and this is caused by a sluggish economy. Inflation is still serious despite price and income controls. In these circumstances we undertook to encourage business investment. Again, this is a longer term route, though we sincerely hope business will have the courage to anticipate the economic recovery and expand production immediately.
Looking at the situation in its entirety, though, we have a responsibility to all Canadians and it is one which 1 feel the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) has conscientiously discharged in the drafting of this budget. He has done it well and honestly in very difficult circumstances and without bowing to the easy solutions which the opposition would have us believe would have solved all of our problems.
The leader of the loyal opposition in Manitoba, Sterling Lyon, and the minister of labour in the Manitoba government, Russ Paulley, were for once agreed that larger tax cuts were called for, according to reports in the Winnipeg press. First of
The Budget-Hon. J.-P. Guay
all, we did what we could to put more money into the hands of Canadians. But beyond that, we recently provided some large tax room to the provinces in the order of $700 million. We can't give away that kind of taxing power to the provinces and still have the same ability left to give Canadians tax cuts.
If the provinces had also provided tax cuts out of their portion of the revenue, the relief for Canadians would have been even more substantial. It is sometimes easy for the provinces to make us appear the bad guys, or to make us look bad, yet they fail to look at their own province and what they are doing for the benefit of Canadians or for the benefit of the people in their own province. Just for example, you do not see any provincial government considering the possibility of taking 5 per cent off the price of a gallon of gasoline. Surely to goodness they could certainly do that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why don't you take off your 10 per cent?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It would be nice to take off 10 cents or 25 cents, but the tax on a gallon of gasoline in Manitoba is one of the highest in Canada, so I think some consideration should be given to reducing their tax. Even if there were a Conservative government in Manitoba, I do not think things would be any better. Certainly, when Roblin was premier the Conservatives did not do any better; in fact, he put the Manitoba government more in the hole than it has ever been. So I will talk about that if the hon. member wants to talk about it. A $6 billion or $7 billion deficit is a fairly powerful stimulus to the economy, but it is still a large deficit and is widely distributed; for example, a mix of job creation, business encouragement, tax relief for Canadians and transfer payments to the poorer provinces of hundreds of millions of dollars.
Under the Prime Minister, the federal government has been accused of being centralized and too inflexible. Let us not forget, Mr. Speaker, that the provinces have absolute responsibility in many areas, the best known of which is education. Let us also not forget that in 1945 the federal government's budget represented 70 per cent of government spending in Canada, whereas in 1977, this year, the provinces and municipalities will account for 70 per cent of spending in Canada. This is quite a change.
Let us also not forget that much of the federal budget consists of transfer payments, not spent by the federal government but money that is put into the hands of the provinces through various grants and programs, or put into the hands of pensioners, the unemployed, Indians and so on. All of these groups spend this money as they see fit, but the federal government gets the blame on budget day.
We have told the provinces that we are ready to negotiate a new formula for taxing. We have had ongoing policies of decentralization of federal departments and services. Moving the head office of the Department of Veterans Affairs to Prince Edward Island is a good example, as is the move of the Mint to Manitoba. But we cannot do everything for everyone overnight. And we are willing to continue trying, to accept criticism and adapt to that criticism. But let the criticism be

April 19, 1977
The Budget-Hon. J.-P. Guay
intelligent, let it be honest, let it be constructive. Very little of this has been coming from opposition benches lately. ,
I should also like to take this opportunity to speak about other matters of great concern to all Canadians at the present time. I should like to speak about national unity and about language rights in Canada. For the benefit of the members of the House I should like to examine the position taken by certain Progressive Conservatives from Manitoba, for example, on these questions, and the inconsistencies in that party's position when elaborated in western Canada as compared to Quebec.
Recently the Prime Minister has been accused of being the cause of separatism in Quebec. We soon forget the bombs in Montreal mailboxes in 1961 and 1962 when the government of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) was in office. There had been dissatisfaction in many parts of French speaking Canada long before the present Prime Minister took office.
Let me just talk about the position of some of the hon. members opposite who come from my own province and their worthy contribution to national understanding and national unity. Many of the present members of that party voted against the Official Languages Act and they continue to work and campaign against the equality of languages in Canada. Yet the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark) goes to Quebec and tells Quebecers that his party supports the Official Languages Act. If it does, Mr. Speaker, it barely does. But barely supporting it will not keep us a united country, a united Canada.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie) is a good example of the intelligence and understanding members of the Progressive Conservative party bring to many issues in Canada, and to the issue of unity most of all. The hon. member says he is not against French in Canada or against French speaking Canadians. Yet he is constantly against any government spending to provide them with services in their own language. I should like to refer to the hon. member's impressive record on this question, taken from his own press release of July 20, 1976. It is interesting to note that the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre is so proud enough of his position to put out a press release on it. The press release is as follows:
Mr. McKenzie stated that his record will show that he has taken a clear stand on bilingualism. First of all, as one of the P.C. members who opposed the Official Languages Act. ..
The Winnipeg PC member then listed some examples of times he had spoken out on bilingualism such as:
1.	Opposition to bilingual labelling and packaging. (Speech March 17, 1975)
2.	Opposition to the fact that CNR employees were not being treated fairly in regards to language training.
3.	That he was the first MP to speak out against bilingual air traffic control services...
In conclusion, Mr. McKenzie said, I think the people of Winnipeg South Centre can see that I have always made clear my opposition to the Liberal government's bilingualism policy.

The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre has an amazing ability to make opposing statements, because in the House on March 7, 1975, as reported at page 4191 of Hansard, the hon. member said:
This bill is the most divisive piece of legislation that has ever appeared on a federal or provincial statute book. It makes a mockery of the Official Languages Act.
Here are a few of the headlines which appeared in the Winnipeg press on various occasions when the hon. member spoke: "McKenzie hits bilingual labelling"; "McKenzie critical of way language training handled".

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: So was Spicer.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Another headline: "CNR's approach to bilingualism attacked". The Leader of the Opposition should take this illustrious member for Winnipeg South Centre with him when he goes to Quebec to campaign in the forthcoming by-elections.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. The minister must refer to an hon. member of the House by his riding, not by his name.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As I was saying, the Leader of the Opposition should certainly take the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre with him when he goes to Quebec, and I am sure there are others who feel the same way he does. It is interesting to me to see the Leader of the Opposition go to Quebec and state that his party is in favour of the government's language policies, while his boys back home vote against them, or deliberately exploit and misrepresent those policies. It may win them some seats in the west, but it could cost us the country in the east. My job and the job of government members is to force these people to stand up and defend their views of Canada.
The hon. member, the Leader of the Opposition, should in fact go to many of these nomination conventions in Manitoba and make it known what his policy is. Then members who will take the convention will also support him in this regard. That will give me the right to believe that the hon. member of the opposition is sincere when he tries to tell easterners that his party is a national party in regard to bilingualism in Canada.
If British Columbia sees Canada as an English country only as a result of the battle on the Plains of Abraham, and they are able to convince people outside Quebec of that view, how can we honestly convince the French speaking of Canada and of Quebec that there is a home for them in this country from sea to sea?
I am sincerely afraid that this hon. member is much more representative of the feeling in his party than is his leader. I am making reference to the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. To prove that he is not alone, I would like to read from an extract of an interview on radio station CKFM of Toronto with Mr. George Henderson, a Progressive Conservative MLA
April 19, 1977

in the province of Manitoba, heard March 1, 1977. Mr. Elenderson said:
No, I don't go along with ... I don't want to deny anybody of their rights . .. but I think our objective... should be to work toward one official language in the years ahead-
The announcer said: "Canada has a serious problem on its hands". Henderson went on to say: "I don't think we have a serious problem in Manitoba".

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. O'Sullivan), on a point of order.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. minister permit a brief question?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will shortly, when I am through. The moral of these lines must be: "None so blind as he who will not see".

Mr. Speaker, as a French-speaking member from the west, from Manitoba, Winnipeg, St. Boniface, I wish to express my views on Canada even if 1 am not a Quebecer. I shall start by quoting the paragraph of the preface in Mr. Keith Spicer's last report, which, 1 think, gives a good summary of the present situation. He says:
When two peoples face each other in complete inequality, the disadvantaged people, seeing no hope of progress, stays resigned and, in a political sense, calm. Then, when the gap of inequality starts closing, and hope and even expectation rise, the disadvantaged tolerate less and less the remnants of injustice. Instead of satisfying their aspirations, progress toward fairness irritates, and a raw-nerve political awareness condemns as an outrage every vestige of the earlier, genuine domination.
At the provincial level in Canada, we see a lot more than a "vestige of genuine domination".
Mr. Speaker, I am from Manitoba. It is the province of Louis Riel, of Fort Maurepas, Fort de la Reine, the voyageurs, and St. Boniface, the cradle of Christian civilization in the west. It is my province and also that of my father and his father. I am a member of parliament and a minister in the federal government and I have fewer rights in Manitoba, which entered Confederation as a province respecting the two major groups in 1871, than would English-speaking Quebecers if the white paper became law. And this in spite of what Mr. Schreyer says in Manitoba when he deals with that matter on the national network. Again I quote Keith Spicer who says on page 8 of his report about the 1,420,760 Canadians of French ethnic origin found outside Quebec in 1971, and I quote:
. . . of the 1,420,760 Canadians of French ethnic origin the 1971 census found outside Quebec, less than 48% still used French at home.
On one hand, their English-speaking neighbours tend to ignore them, tell them to assimilate, or warn them at least not to ask more than "other" local ethnic groups. Usually the same English-speakers who most loudly denounce Bill 22 in Quebec have been leading the fight for years against free choice of decent French schools and against taxpaid services in French-even when the French "minority" population reaches 50, 70, or 90% of a region or town.
Let us consider, Mr. Speaker, the statistics mentioned by Mr. Keith Spicer on page 33 of his report about the percentage of French-speaking federal civil servants:
The Budget-Hon. J.-P. Guay
3.9% in scientific research; 8.2% in biological science; 5.8% in forestry; 5.1% in physical sciences; 10.2% in chemistry; 12.5% in electronics; 8.6% in meteorology; 9.9% in engineering and scientific support; and 7% in aircraft operations.
Those rather low percentages would be even lower if they covered scientists and technicians working for Crown agencies not outside the jurisdiction of the Public Service Commission such as those involved in nuclear and petroleum research.
If French-speaking civil servants get only 22 per cent of federal positions, and if they represent 28 per cent of the population, they register a loss of 6 per cent. The average salary for those positions-as it is mainly in the technical and senior categories that they are underrepresented-is $20,000 a year and there are 400,000 positions in the civil service.
All those figures show that the French-speaking community in Canada gets 400,000 multiplied by 6 per cent which makes
24,000	jobs and 24,000 times $20,000 which this year makes $480 million less than it should get in salaries from the federal government while the English-speaking community receives in addition the equivalent, that is a difference of $1 billion this year alone. How long has this been going on, Mr. Speaker? Was the pilot strike only an opportunity to protect a monopoly of well-paid jobs? Our English-speaking pilots are surely more honest than that. However, a French-speaking pilot could think it is so.
Mr. Speaker, this being said, even if I would have liked to continue speaking on bilingualism, I would like to say a few words about questions which have been put to me and I hope to have enough time to answer.

It might be an appropriate time to discuss my duties in cabinet and answer some of the questions which members opposite have been asking. Generally, my duties are to represent the people of St. Boniface as their member of parliament. My further duties are to be a member, and by definition a western representative in cabinet. A further duty which is far more delicate and onerous in Canada today is to be the only federally elected representative of more than 300,000 Francophones in western Canada. In Manitoba I still do my normal duties as a member of parliament, besides which I now deal with province-wide situations involving Manitoba and their federal government. This is probably more involved in Manitoba where there is only one federal minister and one other government member of parliament.
Manitoba is a large province. I must re-establish contact, as a representative of the federal government and cabinet, with the areas outside Winnipeg and the major towns. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like my colleagues on this side of the House I wonder why the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) bothered to put on that extravaganza on budget night, that charade which masqueraded as the tabling of the budget. I add my voice to the protest which has been raised in the last few days, and I ask why the Minister of Finance did not resign before instead of after budget night. If this budget is his swan song, then I can only suggest that he is tone deaf. He is just as out of tune with the times as his cabinet colleagues, including the Prime Minister.
If the Minister of Finance plans to adopt a new career when he leaves the cabinet, I recommend something other than a career as a juggler. His sleight of hand act on Thursday night was strictly bush league and, as far as I know, he did not fool anyone, with the possible exception of himself.
Budgets are supposed to provide solutions to pressing problems, and the Minister of Finance knows as well as any of us that there are pressing problems to spare. The government creates new problems with every day that passes, and it is time it at least went through the motions of solving a few of them.
The budget does not face up to any of the problems which beg for solutions. It turns completely away from the most immediate and serious problem about which everyone is talking, high unemployment. Saying that it is high unemployment is the kindest way to express it. I am sure that many of those one million unemployed-a large percentage of them chronically unemployed-would have much stronger and harsher words to describe their situation.
The issue confronting Canada today is not separatism, bilingualism, or national unity. The main issue and the main grievance of the people of this country is the collapse of our economy and the many other symptoms which go with that. We have record unemployment. We have no jobs for qualified, willing people. The Prime Minister told them in Toronto that if they want jobs they would have to go to other countries. We have a record high cost of living, with record inflation circumscribing private and personal initiatives. Our outgoing trade is diminishing, and we have record high taxation coupled with the utter ineptitude of the Trudeau government. There is gross mismanagement and waste in government administration. A government which can correct and cure these conditions will have no trouble with social and separatist problems. A thriving economy and busy working people are the best insurance against disunity.
The government makes much of the fact that it is pumping a total of $452 million into its direct job producing programs, Canada Works and Young Canada Works. The Minister of Finance would have us believe that here at last is the magic solution, that everyone will suddenly have a decent paying job, that our young people will be able to plan their lives, and that those who have been bumped out of the labour force will now be welcomed back to their jobs with open arms. But it is not going to be like that at all. What we will get for the $452 million is 150,000 short-term jobs, and the one million unemployed will be virtually unaffected. There will be 225,000 new people moving into the labour force, or should we call it the "looking-for-a-job" force? That means that there will be
75,000	new candidates for the unemployment rolls. It is scandalous.
It appears that my riding will receive about $100,000 in Canada Works funds, and another $60,000 to replace the wharf at Bath. I appreciate that measure because a new wharf at Bath is certainly needed. The one the government built less than a decade ago was poorly planned and badly constructed, so it did not endure against the assault of water and ice in the spring. Of course $100,000 for Canada Works and $60,000 to replace the wharf at Bath is small potatoes compared with what the government is planning to spend in Quebec.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) says that the farmers in Quebec will be getting the lion's share of the increase in subsidies to be paid to farmers under the new dairy policy. The minister admitted that politics was involved in the hike in subsidies, and in the same breath said that the government was not trying to buy votes in the province.
The plain fact is that the government has been involved in buying Quebec votes with the funds in the federal treasury for a very long time, for the full term of the present government. It seems that everyone except the government can see that the results of that policy have led Canada to the brink of destruction. Another example of this is the revival of the capital works program. The program was revived, but only so that another


April 19, 1977
$215 million could be earmarked for federal construction projects in the coming year in Montreal.
I think that these capital projects in Quebec, such as the Montreal and Hull projects, should be stopped until we see what the situation is going to be vis-a-vis Quebec separation. After all, this is not Quebec money that we are talking about, it is money collected from Canadians all across our country. It is another scandal piled on top of a long list of scandals when the government spends hundreds of millions of those dollars in a vain attempt to shore up the sagging economy and its sagging image.
It is time for someone in the country to exercise leadership in this matter of Quebec versus the rest of Canada, and the place to start is to recognize the fundamental fact that Quebec is still a province of Canada and is therefore subject to the laws of Canada and the Canadian Constitution. For several years now Quebec has been telling us what it is going to do, and what we are going to have to do for it. It has been a one-way street, with all of the dialogue directed at what would be best for Quebec rather than at what would be best for the majority of the people of Canada. I have many written protests from the electors in Frontenac-Lennox and Addington regarding this situation. We cannot spend our way out of this situation, and even if we could it would be a fraudulent use of public funds. The funds collected by the federal government, and held in trust for our people, cannot be used for the benefit of a small sector or a small group of our people to the exclusion and the detriment of the rest of the people.
Still another example of this fallacy is the expenditure of billions of dollars on the federal government's bilingualism program. It has been proven beyond any reasonable doubt that the bilingualism program has been, and is, a disaster of monumental proportions. We are not getting value for our money. It has divided the country into linguistic and even racial groupings, and there has never been a government program or project in our history that has been so damaging to human relations in our country. That is why the Prime Minister made apologies for it last night in Winnipeg, as best he could. In spite of all that, the government has budgeted another $405 million for bilingualism in the coming year. This is money down the drain, at a time when the state of the Canadian economy is the worst in the memory of most if not all members of this House. One of the many reasons why our economy is in such bad shape is that Canadians can no longer compete in world markets, or even in their own domestic markets. The people of my riding, Frontenac-Lennox and Addington, are fed up with this condition, and I have many letters of protest.
It has been noted in these debates that the deficit in Canadian foreign trade as of last year was $11 billion. This deficit is increasing at an alarming rate, every day that passes, and I think that we should all be alarmed at the rate at which it is growing. For instance in 1975 the foreign trade deficit was about $5 billion, and one year later it was $11 billion. That is certainly a sure sign that we are in serious trouble-brought on by Trudeau liberal-socialist policies.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before the House rose for dinner I was talking of the sickly condition of the Canadian economy. We used to be a country whose products were in demand all over the world, and that applied to manufactured goods as well as natural resources, raw resources, the export of paper pulp and all grades of paper, including newsprint. Over the past few years we have gradually but surely priced ourselves out of those markets. Our former customers in the United States have been looking around for better deals in these products, and it now appears that the markets for most of our products have been lost to us for all time.
The new suppliers are trying harder to keep their customers than we have done, and a good case in point is the fact that for the fourth year in a row we have been losing customers to German, Japanese and even American suppliers. The cost of production in Canada keeps rising at a faster rate than in any other country, and at present it costs us from 10 to 25 per cent more to produce a product than it costs United States producers to make the same product.
Firms which have deserted Canada for the U.S. claim that it costs 25 per cent less to start up a new industry in the U.S. than it does in Canada, and 25 per cent less to operate, taking into account the costs of labour, materials, energy and taxes. The unions on the one hand, and the Trudeau government on the other, seem to be determined to price Canadian products out of every market left to us and, believe me, there just are not many markets left to us any more. Today's newspapers tell us that the State of Vermont is luring industry away from Quebec and Washington State is attracting industry away from British Columbia.
Last year, for instance, workers in Canadian manufacturing industries received wage increases averaging about 14 per cent; and labour leader Joe Morris wants wage and price controls lifted so that his workers can get even more. They say they will need catch up wage increases to compensate for the wage and price controls of the past two years. Mr. Speaker, that would be a big laugh if it were not so serious. In the United States, where they have not had wage and price controls, the average wage increase for workers in manufacturing industries was below 8 per cent. That is one of the main reasons for their taking away our markets in manufactured products.
Here, in Canada, since the mid-1960's we have seen a rapid expansion in the public sector and a decline in the growth of the private sector. The public sector, the various levels of government, now accounts for about 48 per cent of our gross

April 19, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Alkenbrack
national product, narrowing the field still further for the vital growth factors such as savings, capital investment and exports. We simply cannot continue to operate in this way if we expect to survive as an exporting nation, and that is the only way we can possibly survive. Putting it very simply, we cannot survive unless we export.
The surest sign a country is in serious economic difficulty is when people who work with their own capital begin to leave it, in search of greener investment pastures. We have that situation in Canada right now. Never before in our history has there been such a rush of capital out of the country. It is estimated that last year $1 billion in investment capital went out of Canada to the United States and other countries, but mostly to the U.S. High labour costs, high material costs, high taxes, senseless and harassing government meddling-those are some of the reasons why people with money are packing up and leaving us. The band-aid measures in the budget designed to stem the flow of capital and expertise out of our country fall far short of what is needed. We have arrived at the point where we need a great deal more in the way of inducements than these piddling half measures.
This budget should have set in motion the machinery for scaling down federal government involvement in the national economy. There has to be a turn around in the relationship between public and private sector spending activity. This budget could have been used as the vehicle for announcing a massive cutback in public sector spending, matched by a corresponding reduction in taxes. An acceleration in private sector spending, largely in the investment sector, cannot be initiated without incentives. These incentives must be of such a nature that investors will have confidence not only in our national economy but in our national government as well.
All too often the government has announced incentives, for instance in the way of tax relief, and then either rescinded the measures later or cancelled them out by adding taxes in another area. The budget we are now debating offers band-aid incentives to business, but then it proves beyond a shadow of doubt that the government intends to step up rather than scale down public spending. The ten cents per gallon excise tax on gasoline, for instance, was not rescinded. The government will collect about $750 million this year with that stupid tax which increases the cost of energy.
We find that the federal government, having opted out of succession duty taxes, now plans to tax the proceeds of life insurance policies. As my colleague from Parry Sound-Mus-koka (Mr. Darling) said in his remarks on the budget, the government is reduced to robbing the dead in an effort to grub more money from the already over taxed Canadian taxpayer. That is about the only way to describe the proposal for taxing the proceeds of life insurance policies. Without doubt the government has plumbed the depths of infamy in its tax policies and in the way it has squandered the money squeezed from Canadian wage earners.
Even when the government appears to give the taxpayer a break, there is always a catch. 1 am referring to the proposal to remove capital gains tax from the sale proceeds of a farm or

small business. If you examine that proposal closely you will find that it is only a half measure, one which will allow the government in time to realize a capital gains tax from the sale of a farm or business. For instance, the tax really is only deferred if the proceeds from such a sale are reinvested in another farm or business. An individual or family who worked for 30 or 40 years and wants to sell a farm or business in order to enjoy a few years of retirement will be hit with the tax. In many cases it will no doubt make the difference between realizing, or not realizing, enough from the sale for a family to be able to retire in circumstances that it has a right to expect. In time, even if the proceeds from such a sale are re-invested in a similar enterprise, the government will get its pound of flesh when the business is eventually sold and the proceeds are not immediately re-invested. It is the old story of how this government seeks in every possible way to penalize initiative, resourcefulness, thrift, and free enterprise.
To return to the statements I made earlier with respect to the growth in the public sector, and the impediments that the government places in the path of growth in the private sector, it appears to be a pattern that goes back to the Prime Minister's earlier training and experiences in socialism at the Marxist London School of Economics. Understandably, the Prime Minister has gathered around him a coterie of London School of Economics trained economic geniuses, people who have destroyed more economic systems than any other group of people in the world. To the Prime Minister and his superplanners and the other products of the London School of Economics, socialism is a magic word, the cure-all and the great panacea of the world's economic ills. Well, Mr. Speaker, nine years of that kind of economic gamesmanship have brought us to the brink of moral, political, economic, and social bankruptcy.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the privilege of speaking in the 1977 spring budget debate. In retrospect somewhere down the road, it could turn out to be a very significant budget for this country.
As unorthodox as it may seem, I will try to be brief and stick to the subject. In deference to my good friend, the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. O'Sullivan), I will try to speak without reading, that is, off the cuff. Unfortunately he is not here at the moment.
I have to admit that when I first listened to the budget speech, in contrast to previous budgets, I found this one difficult to assess immediately. Having to make a statement on it to the media, one would have to admit that it required some careful study over a period of time, perhaps a week or so. I think that helped a great deal. Usually with the budget we expect some immediate impact, some characteristic feeling about it. While this budget provided some of this feeling, it required extra study.
This budget tended to continue the shift to a free enterprise type of economy. I consider that all to the good. I hope the members of the official opposition will agree with that.
April 19, 1977

There was a great expectation of certain dramatic moves such as the end of controls and perhaps some sweeping tax cuts, at least for the consumer if not for corporations and for business. That might have been very popular, but I think the feelings about such moves were divided. The results were quite unpredictable. As popular as this might have been, it meant that avoiding these traps was a very courageous move on the part of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald).
With careful study, the thrust of this budget emerges in a number of ways, perhaps half a dozen. First, as I mentioned, there is intended to be less government and more private sector initiative and responsibility. Governments of all kinds feel that desire in the Canadian public and elsewhere. Certainly the Canadian public feels strongly in this way. We have come a long way down the road toward government programs. Many are in place. Now is the time to get back to private initiative.
Second, and this is very important in this time of high unemployment, there is an increasing feeling that we need to create real jobs through investment in the private sector.
Third, we need more regional development on behalf of our fellow citizens in some of the less developed, less industrialized regions. I think all members agree with that.
Fourth, the minister has obviously opted for some specific tax relief, not the broad sweeping changes some expected, but measures that are realistic, possible, hopefully non-inflationary, and of help to those who need help most.
Fifth, there is an honest attempt here to continue implementing government spending restraint to the tune of S650 million, or an annual increase of about 7 per cent, much smaller than in previous years.
Sixth, the anti-inflation fight continues because there must be no end to the controls before there is a commitment on the part of everyone to continue in the spirit of voluntary restraint.
Seventh, there is a call in a general sense for business, labour, and all sectors of the Canadian public to work together on Canadian problems.
Every time there is a budget, and this one is no exception, there is a tendency to describe it in a derogatory way as a do-nothing or stand pat budget. 1 do not believe it is that. For those who take a careful and intelligent look at it, it is a budget that requires some study and interpretation.
There are two problems. It is a very technical budget in terms of measures introduced. Second, it returns a great deal of the initiative in solving our problems, particularly economic problems, productivity, industrialization, jobs, in fact the whole package, to the private sector where it belongs. As a rider to this aspect, the important point is the follow-up. In this case the government has not said it is going to spend so much and going to accomplish so much. It said it would open the doors to the private sector. They now have the opportunity to do what they said they wanted to do. It will take at least six months to get some kind of response and results.
This general approach back to the private sector, free enterprise, is not one which will please our socialist colleagues
The Budget-Mr. Philbrook
in the House. That is not their way of thinking or doing things.
I do not believe it is the way this Liberal party is going in the future. However, 1 have difficulty understanding when our Conservative colleagues tend to criticize a budget or thrust like this roundly.
I will give some reactions to this later, but I would like to quote now from a man who said this budget is honest medicine. He said that he did not think he would be the only person supporting the federal budget "when the smoke clears away in the few days," that is, after the budget had been presented. He said the cure lies in improving the country's competitive position in world trade. We have to be very leary of revitalizing the inflationary pressures that are still there. He applauded the federal decision not to reduce its sales tax. How much more do we want to stimulate consumer spending? "It is good. Our expectations are already too high." The man who said this is the treasurer of the Ontario government, Mr. Darcy McKeough. He is not considered a Liberal and is many times a critic of this particular government's policies. In this case, however, he is right in line. He also said, in the face of criticism from the leader of the NDP in Ontario, that he would have us in the same mess that the United Kingdom is in, dragged down by socialist policies.
His boss, the premier, said he wants to see plans for the post-control period before the anti-inflation program is removed. In this case we have a pretty solid endorsement for this budget from the Ontario government.
From the first there has been one thing that disappoints the suburban riding of Halton and its member of parliament. This is not entirely unpredictable. It is the fact that there was no mention of support, or even a spirit of suppport, for financial assistance to commuter transit such as the GO train in Ontario. I will not go into that subject in great detail because it has been covered in a previous speech. But I thought it would be in the spirit of working through the private sector in terms of boosting Canadian industry, rail cars, buses, and so on, and also in the spirit of energy conservation.
What, then, is the general thrust? It is designed to be in favour of private business and of the economy in general, and also in favour of people, in the sense that they are not separate; they are inseparable, and our best hope of creating employment-the minister has seen this and has done his best to implement it in difficult financial conditions-is to create employment through the private sector. To do this, we have to boost the economy. We have done this in several different ways-in terms of tax changes, to encourage risk taking, and particularly to encourage small business in Canada, in addition to the other thrusts, having a minister for small business, less paperwork and all the rest of it, tax relief for families hardest hit by inflation, and increased employment expense deductions. I shall not go into this in detail because these things have been set out in pamphlets and so on.
The creation of employment is to be done, as we have said, not by government jobs, not by Canada Works programs and

April 19, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Philbrook
so forth, which we now realize are very limited, important as they are, but through investment in the private sector. This makes for real, long term jobs. Other measures include boosting the equity market, the cash flow, the sort of thing business needs to thrive and compete overseas or, at least, to compete here in Canada against imported goods.
Then there is the aspect which is so difficult and upon which we all agree, I think, that of helping regional growth, particularly in the maritimes. Even here, in terms of creating jobs through investment rather than through government, it might not be the NDP approach usually. But when we were discussing the transit policy I noticed encouragement even from that quarter when the members of this party wanted the growth of business, and real jobs, because they did not seem to want handouts.
I do not want to be repetitious and go into all the various points of this budget. Very briefly, to set the stage, there are at least ten different ways in which the budget attempts to help the business community. First, there is an investment tax credit which is not only being continued but is being extended for the needy regions and for research and development in science and technology, which is a great boost for this country. Second, there is 3 per cent inventory deduction. Third, there is an increased dividend tax credit. Fourth, capital gains are included in the $1,000 exemption. Fifth, there is the provision affecting stock dividends for public corporations. Sixth, there are some income tax changes and, it is to be hoped, a simpler income tax process involving much less paperwork. Seventh, there is provision for easing the cost of metric conversion. Eighth, stock options for private Canadian companies, not just for executives but for any and all workers. Ninth, gains on Canadian securities are to be taxed at a lower rate. Tenth, provision is made for deferred taxes on reinvestment with particular reference to farms and small business-this can only be a very welcome move, and, finally, increased sales tax exemptions.
There is certainly enough there to make business interested, and we have reason to expect a good response from business. If we get that response, we hope there will be even more consideration extended with a view to helping make this economy what it should be.
As for the general public, although there may not be sweeping changes, big tax cuts, there are temporary tariff reductions, job creation measures under the Canada Works program costing $100 million-but that is to be added to more than $450 million, making more than half a billion dollars, which is not insignificant in terms of government job creation on a temporary basis in difficult times.
Finally, I would call attention to the exercise of restraint in government spending. I think this deserves great credit. It had to be a great struggle no matter who was involved.
The theme is for government to encourage a combined effort between business and union leaders to fight inflation and to stimulate increased growth through investment. It is bound to take a great effort of will on the part of all Canadians,

particularly Canadian leaders who have often in the past found themselves on opposite sides of the argument.
Of equal importance is the negative aspect of the budget, in a healthy sense, the traps which have been avoided. Here again the minister deserves credit for his courage in avoiding more government spending in areas where there is always great pressure, avoiding more protectionism for our weaker industries and avoiding a premature ending of controls, something which is really not wanted by the provincial governments or by the small business community as represented by the CFIB under the well known John Bullock, and probably not wanted by the majority of Canadian people, if we can believe the polls.
I have already made reference to unemployment. It is a difficult situation. It is an unusual situation compared to experiences in the past-it is certainly capable of a very different analysis from that applicable to the depression of the 1930's. Unfortunately, there has been a great deal of misunderstanding in this field. I believe the minister has been maligned. I notice one headline saying "The Job Problem Will Remain". I think the writer ought to have added the words "for now" because there are many recent studies, reliable studies, to indicate that this is a temporary problem which will end with the 1980's . The most recent study comes from the Ontario Economic Council and I believe it is encouraging to those who want to look at all the facts. Also, this is a world-wide problem and I think we are tackling it as well as anyone could.
The subject of controls is a very interesting one, too, because of the pressure upon the government to remove them. There was an article in the Toronto Star of March 24 entitled "Big Business and Big Labour Can Wait". It talked about a new alliance to end controls, the famous group of union leaders and businessmen. The article asked: Whom do they speak for? Who is running this country anyway? That is a good question and I think that with this budget we once again know who is running the nation. It is the Government of Canada. These controls must not be removed, much as we dislike them, much as we want to get rid of them, until we have a pretty convincing agreement on voluntary restraint.
Again I return to my favourite point. I find it disappointing that there hasn't been some mention of support for urban transit. This is a view with which I understand at least one person agrees, the head of the Liberal party in Ontario, Stuart Smith.
Public reaction to the budget is very interesting. I do not think there is any question but that it has been well received by the business community, perhaps not as well by others, but certainly by those interested in business economics. I might mention again the reaction of Darcy McKeough of the Ontario government. Ron Anderson, a writer on economics, referred in the Globe and Mail to a re-establishment of the business relationship, that is with government, of course. William Daniel, the president of Shell, said that we had "bitten the bullet" and that this would pay off. Forrest Rogers of the Bank of Nova Scotia called it a "sober but constructive budget in difficult times". A large group of bond dealers showed a
April 19, 1977

positive reaction to the budget and called it a tough, anti-inflationary budget, and applauded its tone. Jeff Carruthers of the Globe and Mail said the write-off scheme should boost frontier oil and the search for new gas supplies. F. H. McNeil, chief executive officer at the Bank of Montreal, was quoted as saying that regional incentives are better than subsidies which generally get wasted.
A large group of top executives in Canada were quoted as being in support of the budget. I mentioned Ronald Anderson of the Globe and Mail a minute ago. He is also quoted as saying that the incentives for investment provided in the budget are the soundest approach to job creation, even if there is an inevitable lag before the effects are felt in the labour market. I. H. Asper was also reported in the Globe and Mail as saying that it has taken nearly two weeks but has finally sunk into the consciousness of Canada's tax watchers that the budget contains such fundamental and important restructuring of the tax system that it will surely be looked back on as one of the most important.
A group of economists gave the budget a passing grade and said that it was preparing for the day of recovery. The Globe and Mail lead editorial on April 1 said the budget was important if it works, that it was courageous. The Canadian Manufacturers' Association applauded the thrust of the budget and said it would control inflation and reward industry. The petroleum industry was pleased with the frontier incentives. Apparently there was a positive reaction from the stock market, according to Crang and Ostiguy. Through CFIB, John Bullock, on behalf of small business, said the budget helps and that we will be happy to keep controls. Then finally, Mr. Sam Hughes, of all people, of the Chamber of Commerce, who has often been a very strong government critic, said the budget was good for business and for the economy.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh yes?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
A welcome back to the hon. member. There were, of course, some reactions against the budget. Apparently there was disappointment among oilmen who regretted the failure to make provincial royalties deductible at last-an old argument. Then, of course, union officials disapproved. Some of the leaders of the NDP, both provincial and federal, disapproved, as did some reporters, such as Geoffrey Stevens, who said it was a cruel budget and accused the Liberal government of "out-torying the Tories". Some of the unemployed, of course, were disappointed. But this is a rather interesting group. I have cited and it is perhaps as much a reflection on their ideas and attitudes and their failure to take a general long-term look at the whole situation as it is upon the budget itself.
Personally, Mr. Speaker, I have not found a great deal of public reaction to the budget, which is strange unless it is because of the point 1 mentioned earlier, that it will take time to see what are the results of the budget. So perhaps that is a good thing. Other budgets have suggested immediate promise
The Budget-Mr. Kempling
and have been disappointing. Where there has been reaction from constituents I have found it mainly on two points. The first had to do with the RHOSP changes; some had taken advantage of the loopholes which are now blocked. The second had to do with estate tax, which in recent years we had avoided.
I think the consensus is that the important thing is the follow-up, the response that we get from the private sector to the opportunities provided by the budget, such as the opportunities to invest, to strengthen business, to boost the economy, to create jobs, and all of this through the private sector.
The media also quoted the Minister of Finance as saying that it is a waiting game; that he will watch the economic indicators, but that if necessary, several months down the road-it is not very long and we cannot afford to wait very long-there will be more additional direct federal expenditure in the autumn, perhaps through the supplementary estimates. I take it that means more government spending, more direct government action to create jobs, and so on. If this is the case it will be a very unfortunate turn of events for this country. 1 think our best course now is the one that has been indicated- job creation through the private sector, through business and industry, without government involvement.
As to anti-inflation controls, Mr. Speaker, it seems evident that the intention is to phase these out as soon as possible, because whether we need them or not they are not going to work in the long term. "As soon as possible" seems to be late in 1977, according to the minister, whether or not business or labour co-operate. I think that is also a very sound move.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, if there is one major reaction to the budget in a surburban riding like Halton it has to be in terms of commuter transit, our hope to enlarge our public transit system through the provincial Go-train system. 1 have mentioned the changes necessary in Union Station and the railway bottleneck nearby at Bathurst. These matters are urgent. Perhaps the money is available and there will be commitments in the near future; in the meantime we had hoped to see some mention of this in the budget. I think there is a sincere desire on the part of the people of Halton riding to work through the private sector and participate in some kind of industrial strategy which is going to get the country moving again in the free enterprise sense.
