subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth recognized that.
The tragedy of the budget presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) is that he lost another opportunity to set the Canadian economy on a straight course to recovery. There have been several lost opportunities. One was when the anti-inflation legislation was introduced. It could have been a pattern for national unity. It could have been a call to the people of Canada to pull together and overcome inflation. It could have called upon all levels of government to reduce spending and ease the tax burden on all citizens. Instead it has become a document that has created terrible disunity in Canada. That is why we are calling for an end to the AntiInflation Board.
The consensus gap between the federal government and the provincial governments has widened; the debate on resource taxation has continued with no resolution in sight. Election promises on urban transit funding have been withdrawn, and months of planning at the provincial and municipal levels frustrated The extension of urban transportation to aid in energy conservation has been brushed aside.
The government, Mr. Speaker, through the Minister of Finance had an opportunity to set us on a straight course to economic recovery. We have a net outflow of investment capital from Canada because of high taxation and a depressed economy, and many investors in Canada, both large and small, have lost confidence in our economy and the government's ability to set it straight. In view of these facts, these investors have taken two decisions: either invest money offshore, outside of Canada, or leave it in the bank and play the short-term investment game.
The action taken by the minister in the budget is better than nothing, but it is totally inadequate to deal with the serious problems we face. The relief given to small business is long overdue. At least it gives the Minister of State (Small Businesses) (Mr. Marchand) something to say, something to work on, but it is not enough to stimulate the small business community. It will do little to cut into unemployment or increase productivity. In fact this is the first budget that I can recall where the government is planning for increased unemployment. The government plans to spend $4.4 billion on unemployment in fiscal 1977, and $5,055 million in fiscal 1978.
The job creation features of this budget are a little more than a sham. They will not create sufficient unemployment to take care of the new people entering the job market, let alone provide employment for any immigrants who may come to Canada. In fact I thought the thoughtless comment of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), when he was discussing the

unemployment matter with some university students and he suggested they should look outside the country, deserves some kind of a medal for intemperate and thoughtless remarks. It was totally uncalled for. I have said that the tragedy is in the opportunities lost by this government.
Let me turn to some positive suggestions that I think should have been and could have been in the budget. Had the minister acknowledged that we have more than 1,300,000 unemployed, he could have said our budget would be designed to deal with this serious problem. Rather than pay out an increasing amount of taxation in unemployment benefits, he could have said that we are going to put in place taxation incentives to encourage the private sector to expand and employ more of the people who are presently without jobs. He could have said that the revenue realized from the capital gains tax is much less than we anticipated when it was put in place, therefore we were going to rescind this tax. He could have said that we were going to encourage investment in small business. We need venture capital in this field.
The minister could have allowed the creation of small business investment corporations where a 100 per cent writeoff would be allowed and where taxation would apply only when earnings are realized. He could have convened a conference of finance and resource ministers to work out a balance of taxation that would encourage and stimulate resource development and parallel research and development policies to ensure their competitiveness. He could have allowed more research and development incentives to industry to allow them to upgrade their plant products and machinery and technical skills so as to be better equipped to compete in the export market. He could have announced the convening of federal, provincial, and municipal conferences to work out ways and means of reducing the tax burden on the tax producers of this nation, because that is a very serious problem. He could have looked seriously at the concept of zero budgeting at all levels of government and taken the initiative at the federal level to try it on a trial basis in certain departments.
Had the Minister of Finance said we were going to aim at a balanced budget in five years' time and we would make every effort to reach that goal, had he said we would endeavour to cut unemployment by two thirds in that five-year period and work toward making the unemployment insurance fund actuarially sound, where the contributions are in balance with the payout or as close to it as we can get, it would have contributed to a feeling of confidence in the country. Had he announced that he would introduce into the House of Commons for debate Canada's position, aims and objectives at the GATT conference in Geneva, so that industry will know the direction in which we are moving, he would have been applauded from coast to coast.
At this time our industry is operating in the dark. Letters received by many members of this House from industries in their constituencies indicate the complete and utter frustration they are experiencing with our GATT negotiations. Faced with high taxation, controls on profit, high interest rates, and inadequate depreciation allowances, industry has reacted with
April 19, 1977

cutbacks in new plant and machinery development, cutbacks in research and development, reduced employment, and a pause in future planning.
What would the reaction and outcome have been had the minister done this? What would the reaction have been had he taken those positive positions I have just put forward? I believe there would have been a very positive reaction. I believe there would have been a feeling of confidence spread across the country. There would have been a pause and reflection by those who are investing offshore, and a recommitment to Canada and its future. With an upsurge in confidence in the future economy of this country, the Bank of Canada could have pursued an appropriate monetary policy because there would have been a tremendous increase in the velocity of money presently in circulation.
If the Minister of Finance had said in clear open terms, "To hell with socialism; this is a free enterprise economy and only by encouraging and re-enforcing the private sector can we adequately deal with unemployment, trade deficits, balance of payments deficits and inflation,"-had the minister and the government had the courage to say that, there would have been a positive reaction right across the country. But this was not the case.
The government still listens to and is motivated by socialists. If the taxation load continues and government spending at all levels increases, there will be no wealth to redistribute. The government could have moved to decrease spending rather than increase it by almost 10 per cent. It could have reduced taxation beyond that announced in the budget and worked on the take-home pay concept rather than continue the AIB wage controls and profit controls. No, Mr. Speaker, this budget does not deal with the realities of the situation in Canada. Spending $8 million to give employment to 1,000 people under so-called tough conditions could have been better placed to retrain hard core unemployed in useful and productive employment. Spending $4.4 billion on unemployment payments has to be a terrible indictment of this government by its own admission.
There are people who hold a genuine fear for the future of Canada. They see little hope for the regional disparities we face, little hope for improvement, and little hope that four or five or ten years down the road actions taken today will lead to an improvement in these areas. The same uncertainty is evident in our universities in research and development. Their research and development are being frustrated by lack of funding, and long term planning is impossible.
We should be looking at a massive effort into the technology required to bring the tar sands on stream. Most of the cost of a barrel of tar sands oil is in taxation, royalties, and interest on the cost of plant and machinery. Would it not make more sense to tackle this problem openly to relieve the energy costs we face, rather than say we will continue to pay more and more for fossil fuels as stated in the budget? Would it not be more realistic to end the confrontation with the maritimes over offshore resources and give them a realistic base for their economy, than to continue to pursue the present policies of this government? Should we not be committed to a maritimes
The Budget-Mr. Kempling
region that is self-sufficient, strong and economically viable, rather than one that must beg, bargain, and barter politically for handouts from the federal government?
The opportunities lost by the minister and the government will leave a scar on the social fabric of the country for years to come. The people are crying out for a change in direction. They want hope for a reasonably secure future. They are angered at the pious statements by responsible government leaders who say Canadians are living too high off the hog. They are sick at the sight of a government that refuses in practice to curb its own appetite for tax dollars. They know that the events in Quebec on November 15 last resulted from the frustrations of the citizens of that province with a government that was corrupt and unable to handle the economy of the province and keep people employed.
The people of this country are angered at the central government for its continued invasion of their privacy, for the continued erosion of their savings, for the political gamesmanship of confrontation with the provinces, for not realizing the difficulties faced by the urban centres in Canada, for the continued attack on free enterprise and the profit motive, and for the indexing of pensions for senior civil servants and members of this House and the Senate. Yes, Mr. Speaker, the people of Canada are angry. They are angered and frustrated at a government that lacks a sound energy policy, and that refuses to state clearly its position on the future of nuclear energy. They are frustrated that it refuses to move to put some clarity and reason into the ongoing debate on the disposal of nuclear waste, and that allows outright misinformation and uninformed views to have a broad public platform and inflame a highly technical subject for which reasonable answers and solutions are available. The anger runs deep and it will take years to dispel.
It used to be said that the twentieth century belonged to Canada, that this was a country with a great future, and that Canadians were an energetic, productive, and intelligent people. Today we see division, separation, discontent, frustration, misunderstanding, confrontation, and an endless number of pressure groups. We have people who are stimulated toward unrealistic expectations by lotteries, where the odds on winning are unbelievable. We have a country that is being run more and more by regulations and rules that are changed without reference to parliament, where the regulations have the force of statute, and those who make the regulations are not accountable to parliament and the people of Canada.
There are thousands of people in the business community who have contributed to the economy with their skills and enterprise. All they want is a chance to continue to see the benefits of their efforts accrue to them. Like them, I fear for the future of this country. They are tired of the cheap political opportunism. They are tired and angered at the nameless, faceless bureaucrats who guide this country and who write legislation continually reinforcing through regulation the power of the bureaucracy. They are angry at highly paid bureaucrats who show their arrogance by indexing their own

April 19, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Kempling
pensions. They are fed up to the teeth with the bureaucratic flatulence and puffery they read in government releases.
People I talked to before this budget was brought down were hopeful for changes. They said, "Surely we have hit bottom. Surely now they'll come to grips with the problems. Surely the experiment with socialism is over and a lesson has been learned". That is what they were saying. The budget did little or nothing to change the scene, and the government stands condemned before the people of the country.
I despair at the conduct of business of this House, at the secrecy, at the manoeuvring, at the endless reports and studies that never see the light of day. I am disgusted at the argument put forth that we cannot touch certain spending estimates because they are enshrined in statutes. In the commercial world anyone who rested his case on that would be relieved of his responsibility.
When we are presented with a national problem we cannot openly discuss it because the government shrinks from open discussions-rather, it takes refuge in consultants and commissions. "Put it to a consultant or a commission", they say, "and remove it from the House of Commons". That is a standard tactic.
The committees of this House are underutilized. They have little or no authority. Watch the gamesmanship at a committee. There is a two-hour meeting. The minister arrives late- there is not a quorum, so 30 or 45 minutes are lost. Then the minister reads an opening statement-another 15 minutes down the drain. I am convinced that many of these moves are planned because the objective is to cut down the time allowed for questioning. Watch the clock, is the criterion for many committee meetings. Stall, drag it out, frustrate them, then when you want the bill through committee stage, schedule three sittings a day and wear the members down with the pressure of time. We have seen it happen.
I have sat on a committee and have seen a minister with 25 aides from his department in attendance. At one meeting I estimated there were half a million dollars in salaries sitting there, watching the clock, and playing the game.
If this continues, if the secrecy continues, if the manoeuvring continues, then whatever relevancy still remains in this House will be lost forever. Democracy as we know it will be gone, and we will become a people possessed by an all-powerful bureaucracy.
Let me turn now to research and development. The Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Faulkner) dealt with this in his remarks in this debate. But, Mr. Speaker, he missed the point completely. He dealt extensively with statistics of the percentage share of research and development of industry, government, and the universities. He then went on to describe the historical background of research and development in Canada. Well, Mr. Speaker, the minister was merely jawboning. What he said is well known. What he did not say is that the total effect of the budget allowances for research and development combined with Bill C-26 is that there will be less

/ money available for research and development in the period ahead.
The make or buy policy of the government will in time diminish the role of the provincial research foundations. Only 1 per cent of our industry can become involved in the make or buy policy of the government.
What the minister should be saying is what he and the department will do about the decline in industrial research from 1.2 per cent to 0.7 per cent of sales. He should explain how, when ITC cancelled the IRDIA program which gave a 25 per cent contribution to research, the 5 per cent on capital cost allowance can replace the 25 per cent given under IRDIA. He should explain that when cutback spending was called for, the lump sum represented by IRDIA happened to be equal to the amount the department was instructed to cut from its spending. That is how IRDIA was really cancelled. The minister should also explain how he could possibly say in his remarks that the 3 per cent inventory adjustment will benefit research and development. It has no relationship to it whatsoever.
Perhaps the minister will explain how he sees the Enterprise Development Program can replace PAIT. After all, PAIT did have a precise direction, but the Enterprise Development Program is a slush fund that has no technological objectives.
The Minister of State for Science and Technology was playing loosely with some dubious statistics. What he could have told us is how this government, this budget, and the Minister of State for Science and Technology will deal with the $10 billion deficit we have in manufactured products. How will this be dealt with and what changes can we expect in the near future? That is the central question, Mr. Speaker.
In the current world trading environment, customers for manufactured goods are placing growing emphasis on product quality and performance and are unwilling to accept inferior products based on obsolete technology, even when there is a considerable price differential. In order to compete in the international market place we must have a high degree of product specialization. That specialization must be supported by a strong technology that flows from an industrial science policy.
We are not competitive in export markets-we have given up 25 per cent of our domestic markets to imports. We have trade missions travelling all over the world seeking out export markets. But surely you realize that export markets for manufactured goods can only be developed from a strong domestic base. Many of our traditional resource markets have been eroded due to competition and low productivity from worn out plants. Probably the pulp and paper industry is the best example. In Quebec we note that 60 per cent of their pulp and paper plants are more than 40 years old.
The need for a comprehensive industrial strategy has been recognized for several years. The development of a strategy that would employ some of the million plus unemployed must be reinforced by a comprehensive research and development policy. Such a policy should be designed to work closely with
April 19, 1977

the provincial jurisdictions. It should complement their efforts and reinforce the base of their economic planning.
When working with limited resources for research science, funding policies should be designed to put the maximum amount of money to work rather than create unwieldy bureaucracies that siphon off research funds and, in effect, reduce the amount of money available for actual research.
Without adequate research and development in our industries we can never hope to close the gap in balance of payments or cover our trade deficit. Without a massive increase in research and development, we cannot hope to create the new jobs required to reduce the number of unemployed.
The minister could have gone much farther than he did and encouraged industry to make more in Canada, to commit itself to a sound secondary industrial base that would encourage new ventures for Canadian made products to offset our balance of payments deficits.
The minister has failed to recognize the technological limitations of the Canadian manufacturing industry. His policy, or lack of policy, bears this out. The primary limitation arises from the extreme fragmentation of the manufacturing firms in Canada. The median firm in Canada has 11 employees. When you examine the employment data, you see that 50 per cent of all employment is in firms having fewer than 270 employees. Fewer than 3 per cent of manufacturing firms currently maintain an in-house research and development activity. The median size research and development activity consists of two qualified scientists or engineers. It is obvious that units of such a small size are only marginally viable. Past and present research and development policies of the federal government are only applicable to 5 per cent of all manufacturing firms. We must conclude that a major effort must be made to serve the needs of the remaining 95 per cent.
We cannot compete with our domestically manufactured products against imports, and we are not able to compete in the international market. We are in the fourth year of underutilization of our economic potential. Our largest customer to the south is in its third year of growth above expectation. If their market runs on its normal five year cycle and turns down for a period of adjustment, whatever benefits flow from this budget will be lost.
The concept we must encourage is savings, and investment that is transferred into plants and increased production. There must be a return of confidence in the market place. We cannot finance industrial development through short term high interest bank loans. It must come from long term investment with a potential of capital gain. Only the producers of wealth can create investment, and we just cannot expand industry on short term bank financing.
I am disgusted at the forecasted increase in government spending. To continue to take 43 per cent of the gross national product to run all three levels of government is ridiculous. That money would be better spent by the taxpayers on private investment in Canada.
The Budget-Hon. J. C. Munro
I am fearful of what lies ahead. This government still has a mandate to govern. I only hope and pray that it will have the political courage to deal realistically with the serious difficulties which exist in the time left in its mandate, but at this time with this budget I see no evidence. Therefore I cannot support the budget as presented by the Minister of Finance on behalf of the government.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of Labour):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as Minister of Labour I am particularly sensitive to the present level of unemployment, which increased to the unacceptable level of 8.1 per cent of the labour force last month. A high level of unemployment is a weakness which has affected all the industrial countries over the last year or two.
Among all the industrial countries Canada is probably the most vulnerable to the recent slowdown in economic activity. Canada must absorb each year the highest proportion of new workers into the labour market. In recent years we have absorbed the largest percentage increase and the largest absolute increase in new workers.
A comparison with other countries gives an indication of the effects of the demographic structure of the country on employment. The OECD has forecast that for the ten year period ending in 1980 the population of working age will increase by 30 per cent in Canada. This is the greatest increase of any of the industrialized countries. The United States is in second place with an increase of 18 per cent, followed by Italy with 8 per cent, France 6 per cent, and finally West Germany and Great Britain with only 2 per cent. One can understand in this context the impact on employment of any weakening of the national economy.
There is another factor which affects employment. I am referring to the increase in prices in a country such as Canada which exports one quarter of its gross national product. Our first deficit in our commercial balance of payments since 1960 appeared in 1975, and this was a troublesome indicator.
Fortunately we experienced a surplus in our commercial account in 1976, but a surplus of $1.3 billion last year represented only half the average annual surplus of our commercial balance in the years 1970 to 1974.
During 1976 the rate of increase in wages was clearly moderating. In the second quarter of 1975 wage settlements in major collective agreements were running at a rate of 18.8 per cent. Since then there has been a significant and persistent downward trend. In the fourth quarter of 1976 new settlements averaged 8.3 per cent, and the trend appears to be levelling off in the first quarter of 1977.
While the Anti-Inflation Board has had a moderating effect on the increase of wages and salaries in current dollars, the improvement in the price performance has effectively brought about dramatic gains in real earnings.
Year over year increases in real weekly earnings-that is the industrial composite-for the third and fourth quarters of 1976 were 4.8 per cent and 4.7 per cent respectively. In the third quarter of 1975, just prior to the introduction of the AIB, the increase was only 2.5 per cent. The 12 month change in
4798

April 19, 1977
The Budget-Hon. J. C. Munro
real weekly earnings to January, 1977, was much more moderate at 2.1 per cent. This, then, reflects partly the increase in the rate of inflation and partly the continuing moderation of the rate of increase of earnings in current dollars.
Real personal disposable income per capita increased by 3.7 per cent in 1976. Prices may not decelerate during 1977 to assure higher rates of increase in real wages and salaries. However, personal disposable income in current dollars should improve with the reduction of personal income taxes as a result of higher personal exemptions and the reduction of the rates of unemployment insurance contributions.
Labour's share of the national income reached an all-time high of 73.2 per cent in 1976. This is part of the long term upward trend in labour's share from approximately 65 per cent in the mid-1950's. Shares of national income and their movements are good indicators, in the short term, of the stages of the business cycle. That labour's share is unusually high at this time indicates that the business sector has been experiencing some difficulty. Corporate profits have declined not only in their share of national income but in their actual level as well. This should be a matter of concern for the labour sector since the ultimate responsibility for job creation lies with the business sector, where profits have traditionally been a major source of investment funds.
It is a fact that Canada has become non-competitive in some of its foreign markets. The increase in wages and salaries in some of our industries has surpassed the increase in wages and salaries elsewhere, notably in the United States, that being our prime trading partner. An economy which depends, as the Canadian economy does, on foreign trade cannot allow itself such a luxury. If this situation were allowed to persist, it would completely undermine the national economy.
Despite the unacceptably high level of unemployment, the national priority continues to be the fight against inflation. The only way to protect jobs and to maintain a high level of employment in this country is to keep our prices competitive with those of other countries or, more precisely, more competitive with our principal trading partners.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Come on, John.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Somebody said, "Come on, John," but talk to the secondary manufacturing firms in the Hamilton area and tell them what it means in terms of unemployment and lay-offs. Tell the workers there about when we become uncompetitive, and they will not be quite so blase about facts and figures such as these.
I think it would be totally irresponsible to end the anti-inflation measures abruptly unless voluntary restraint were agreed to by business and labour in advance, or there was agreement on some kind of monitoring agency. If the government were to end controls abruptly, that could lead to a resurgence of inflation and consequently a drastic cut-back in our exports and worse unemployment for Canada.
With the greatest possible circumspection I would like to consider for a moment certain criticisms which came from the

labour movement immediately following the announcement of the budget by my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald). According to the labour movement, the budget demonstrates the government's indifference to the economic and social hardships of Canadians. The government has been anything but indifferent. It would, on the contrary, be inexcusable or impossible to comprehend if the government were to adopt thoughtless or rash measures.
One could, for example, abolish immediately the entire control mechanism over wages, salaries, and prices, but since wage and salary earners represent 73 per cent of the total national revenue, one can imagine how devastating a new outbreak of rising prices would be for those workers. A return to the kind of inflation we had in the fall of 1975 could destroy all the gains which have been made, gains such as a lower rate of price increases and improved real income over the last 18 months.
If we were to make the Canadian economy non-competitive in foreign trade, we would only be increasing unemployment and we could be accused of adopting an inconsistent economic policy. The leadership of the trade union movement would be the first to lay blame on us-with some justification. We would only incur higher levels of unemployment if we were to end controls, particularly without some kind of voluntary restraint in their place, as we are being urged to do by the labour movement and consumers in the community.
The budget aims to sustain the efforts to lower inflation. The success of 1976 might not be easily repeated since we are faced with rising food and energy prices. Also the lower exchange rate, while stimulating exports and output, will make imports more expensive. A more expansionary policy could not be pursued without creating inflationary pressures and a deteriorating balance of payments situation.
During 1976 while growth in the national product and employment was somewhat erratic, the rate of increase in the consumer price index was gradually declining. In the fourth quarter of 1976, the year over year increase of the consumer price index was 5.9 per cent compared to 10.1 per cent in the fourth quarter of 1975 when we brought in controls. A sizeable decline in food prices contributed significantly to this improvement. However, this situation has been changing. In the first quarter of 1977 the food index was 3 per cent higher than the previous quarter. The increase in the food index was attributable to higher prices for fresh produce, coffee, and restaurant meals. Increased prices for gasoline, fuel, and utilities contributed to the increase in non-food items.
A major economic objective of the budget is to create an environment for a steady growth of output and provide jobs, not only to reduce unemployment but to accommodate a growing labour force.
Expenditures are being directed to create employment. The Canada Works program and the Young Canada Works program have been successfully launched. The additional $100 million, to bring the total to $458 million, will produce many
April 19, 1977

jobs for Canadians this year. In addition, the fiscal measures, the many tax reliefs, the tax incentives, the monetary policies, the devaluation of the Canadian dollar and lower interest rates, will stimulate the economy sufficiently to increase employment.
The budget emphasizes the necessity of restoring confidence in investing in Canadian plant and equipment.
I think hon. members will have noticed the gloomy forecast for the Canadian economy made by the Conference Board a few days ago. On the question of how well they thought the economy would go in 1977, 61 per cent of respondents did not expect conditions to improve, and 25 per cent felt conditions would get worse. Only 8 per cent thought the unemployment rate would drop, and the remainder thought unemployment would remain the same or even increase.
Incidentally, 81 per cent of the respondents to the Conference Board's survey thought that the anti-inflation program was moderately successful.
The measures which the budget is calling for to increase investment are the kinds of measures which will also increase employment. But it is important to be prudent in this area because if there were to be a sudden burst of investment, while this would temporarily improve employment it would also bring about a return of undesirable inflationary pressures.
The budget seeks to maintain a judicious balance between stimulating the economy and improving employment while avoiding the return of inflationary pressures. It provides for an increase in dividend tax credit to 50 per cent from 33'/5 per cent. The existing 5 per cent investment tax credit is to be extended an additional three years. The investment tax credit is to be increased in slower growth regions. The budget proposes to reduce taxes of Canadian individuals and corporations by $1.17 billion in 1977-78. This should also encourage a moderate increase in demand while limiting inflationary pressures.
The future employment outlook has been worsened by a decline in the growth rates of non-residential construction and investment in machinery and equipment.
The importance of this easing of investment in productive capacity cannot be over-emphasized. We must look forward to a time when machinery now idle is once again being fully used. In 1974 the economy ran short of physical productive capacity before it ran short of labour capacity. The incentives for investment in this budget are aimed mainly at those regions where the labour capacity has historically exceeded the physical capacity.
Throughout the seventies Canada has experienced higher growth rates in real gross national product than the United States; in 1976 the advantage turned against Canada. Canada's real growth in GNP, after accounting for inflation, was 4.6 per cent in 1976 compared to 6.1 per cent in the United States. Since the bulk of Canadian exports goes to the United States, an improvement in economic conditions there will help to boost the export-oriented businesses in Canada. A decline in the exchange rate has made our products more competitive;
The Budget-Hon. J. C. Munro further improvements in our competitive position will depend a great deal upon our continuing success in reducing the relative costs of production.
1 would like to come now to a point which is particularly important to me, that is, the co-operation among the major interest groups in the economy, those of the labour movement, business and industry, and consumer groups. We have to work out, on a voluntary basis, a process for consultation which will allow us to make the necessary adjustments to our current economic predicament and to prevent disastrous schisms between various elements of society.
My 14-point program on labour affairs is intended precisely to create a consultative council or forum which would provide facilities for bringing together representatives of the various sectors working together to diminish social conflict. The establishment of such a commission would be particularly useful in the difficult period through which we are now passing.
The process of moving out of controls into a decontrol period depends on consultation and co-operation among the various elements in the economy. Only in this way can we avoid a situation of drastic return to inflationary pressures. The 14-point program which the government is advancing to improve the climate and the practice of labour relations in this country will also have a positive impact on our ability to compete in domestic and export markets. It will do this in a number of ways.
It will, for example, go a long way to improve job satisfaction and the dignity of workers. The program includes a proposal for a national safety and health institute, and safety and health committees at the plant level. We cannot have good production when workers are concerned about their health and safety, or when their health and safety are endangered.
The 14 point program will include a quality of working life centre, which will promote experiments in labour-management co-operation, worker participation and various job satisfaction schemes. This will be linked to a voluntary code of good industrial relations practices.
I think that productivity, as well as job satisfaction, would be improved by the introduction of paid educational leave for workers, and by government funding of trade union leadership training. And I believe that we can help to undermine some of the adversary aspects of collective bargaining by the establishment of the proposed collective bargaining information centre, and by expanding the existing advisory services of my department.
Many of these proposals require the active collaboration of labour and business. My officials and 1 are actively seeking this co-operation and participation. I hope we will draw the right conclusions from the present situation and that we will provide ourselves with the flexible and versatile instruments to deal with our complex economic problems. It is for this purpose that I have introduced my 14 point program and it is for this purpose that 1 support the budget of my colleague, the Minister of Finance.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I begin by stating that I consider it both a personal privilege and serious responsibility to speak this evening in this budget debate and, in so doing, to bring forward in this debate at least some of the views of my constituents in Medicine Hat. It seems to me that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) clearly established some priorities in this budget and, by so doing, also established clearly certain inevitable consequences. The top priority spelled out was that Canada's inflation fight must continue and be won. Hopefully most Canadians will recognize this crucial need and give their general support to this end.
The inevitable consequence of this budget priority is that we shall face the continuing and, now, all time high unemployment. Further, the controls program of the Anti-Inflation Board will continue for some indefinite time frame. A further consequence of the unemployment issue is that the cost of maintaining the 1 million or so unemployed Canadians will be enormous and at record levels. The minister was less than specific in suggesting how this expense will be met. One can only assume that it will be borne entirely by the Unemployment Insurance Commission. But these details will not come to the fore for some time, perhaps not until after the next general election. Meanwhile the federal deficit will continue to rise substantially, without apparent control. That our national rate of inflation has again risen to levels attained just before the anti-inflation controls were instituted in October, 1974, is indeed frightening and sobering.
To be more specific, I wish to commend the Minister of Finance for the special emphasis in the budget directed to small business and farmers. It is appropriate that both should be linked together, since society often forgets that farmers are definitely small-sometimes not so small-businessmen. The former minister of finance had difficulty associating farms with small businesses. Both are operated in most cases under a family type of management.
The capital gains tax deferral proposal for farmers and small businessmen is a good feature of this budget, which will be well received, I am sure. I am also sure that this item was included as a direct result of the growing realization of what a vicious and ruthless tax the capital gains tax is, especially after a period of galloping inflation. I am thinking especially of the way the tax affects farm lands. In its short lifespan this tax has already caused severe hardship in the transfer of farm lands to appropriate heirs. Surely this tax is so insidious that parliament should consider the complete abolition of this capital gains tax. In the meantime I ask the Minister of Finance to consider having this new capital gains tax deferral item apply to family farm corporations and partnerships.
As a further interim action, would the minister also reconsider the proposal that the roll-over provisions of the capital gains tax for inter-generation transfer should be available to family farm corporations and partnerships? The former minister of finance would not consider this, because small businesses would have to be included. Since this budget has now accepted the similarities as between farms and small businesses, as is

evident in the new capital gains tax deferral provision, why does the government not extend the roll-over provisions to family farm corporations and partnerships? Surely such a progression would be logical.
Now I should like to refer specifically to the serious drought all across western Canada and make particular reference to our beef cattle industry in the west. Parliament should be aware that there is a serious drought all across the three prairie provinces and in some of the interior of British Columbia. The area in Canada affected really is part of a much bigger and perhaps more seriously affected drought area extending over the western half of the United States. The more seriously affected areas are the west coast states, beginning with California and the northwestern states bordering Canada. This general, widespread continental drought has already been compared to the disastrous ten-year drought of the 1930's when we were in a business depression.
With respect to the lack of soil moisture in western Canada both in cultivated farm lands and grass lands, the present situation is every bit as serious as it was in the two low points of the 1930's, that is to say, 1931-32, and the spring and summer of 1937. However, with respect to surface water on the prairies, which is so necessary for stock watering, the situation now is worse than it was at any time in the 1930's. This, of course, is a personal opinion, but I was there during the dirty thirties. I was 13 years old at the start, and 23 years old when those bad conditions ended.
Without realizing it then I now know that those ten years of my early life shaped my entire life, including my philosophical view of life and, even now, my political philosophy. The present drought will not be the complete disaster for cultivated cereal crops which the drought of the 1930's was, because of the benefits of herbicides, pesticides, and much more efficient tillage and harvesting machinery. This time farmers will not have to share limited soil moisture with weeds, as was the case in the 1930's.
However, for the cattle industry and for prairie grass production-and there are approximately 45 million acres of native grassland in the west-this drought will be just as serious as the one of the 1930's, perhaps more serious, considering that there are now twice the number of cattle on the land. Keep in mind that in all Canada we have available a total of 50 million acres of grassland. Therefore the 45 million acres on our western prairies which are now subject to this potential drought are of special significance.
While there have been numerous, recent comments that we have yet to see a drought in February or March, I point out that we have had two consecutive winter droughts for the last two winters. This accounts for our present serious shortage of surface water. The chances of sufficient rain to produce surface water in the short grass ranches on the prairies are now almost non-existent. The good crops of grain, grass, and hay last year were the timely results of just two general rains in mid-June and August. We were very lucky and very fortunate.
April 19, 1977

1 might point out that essentially there has been no rain since last August, and very, very little snow throughout the past winter. 1 want to point out what this means. Our carrying capacity over those short-grass ranges is about 50 acres per mature animal unit, or 50 acres per cow. Under conditions today, based on the amount of grass that is there, or the amount that is not there, it will require 80 to 100 acres of grass to pasture one cow for a 12 month period. That is approximately two cows per quarter section. Think about that.
What has our prairie cattle industry done in the face of this drought? Calf producers have had no difficulty or hesitation in making the only decision open to them, namely, to reduce their cattle numbers to fit the reduced carrying capacities of their ranges, and this includes the capacity to water their cattle, sheep or horses.
As a consequence of the drought there has been a consistent and steady increase in the movement of cattle off the winter and spring ranges, either directly to feedlots for heavier feeder cattle or to the market for lighter stocker cattle, most of which have been shipped to Ontario.
In a 60 mile strip from Medicine Hat through Walsh on the Alberta-Saskatchewan boundary and ending at Maple Creek, Saskatchewan, there have been some 5,000 to 7,000 of these kinds of cattle per week passing through four auction markets in these three locations. Approximately 50 per cent of these cattle could properly be described as "drought cattle", in this case cattle which would normally not have been moved until next fall after a full summer's growth on grass.
On my own ranch which is north of Walsh on the Alberta-Saskatchewan boundary, during the Easter recess we had to move 336 head of two year olds, including all of my replacement heifers, to a finishing feedlot. Further, we had to sell another 210 short yearling steers last Saturday at an auction in Walsh. That was a very difficult decision to make, to reduce our cattle numbers by over one third, but it was necessary for the simple reason that we could not have watered these cattle for more than another week, and the necessary spring and summer grazing just did not exist. The prospects are not there for it.
Market prices for these drought cattle have been surprisingly strong with 550 pound yearling steers selling to prices of over $44 and a top carload price of over $45.40 per hundredweight. These strong prices clearly reflect the general upturn in the total North American cattle industry. They also clearly indicate that our North American free market system is working and working very well, in spite of very irresponsible statements by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), such as the one he made in Tilley, Alberta, last January 19, just a few miles north of my constituency boundary near the town of Brooks, and quoted in "Canadian Weekend" magazine of March 26. This is a direct quote:
The free-marketing system is as outdated as Jesus Christ-and almost as redundant.
The Budget-Mr. Hargrave
I can assure hon. members that is a quote. Some two and a half weeks earlier the same Minister of Agriculture was quite willing to suggest as his only recommendation for the drought that the members of this House of Commons should pray for rain. That was in response to some very serious questions about the drought put by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and myself.
If cattle producers are to take these severe steps to reduce their cattle numbers, as they are certainly already doing, and this will be at some considerable sacrifice, surely it is not unreasonable for governments to share in some forms of emergency actions.
The suggestion 1 am going to make is not new. It was put forward during our House debate on the prairie grain stabilization bill by my colleague, the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Hamilton). The proposal was to use our federal tax system as the instrument to create incentives by cattle producers on an individual basis to make their own management decisions respecting drought.
These extensive forced sales of drought cattle will create abnormally high gross and net income figures for 1977 and possibly future years if the drought persists. Why not have an extension of the capital gains tax deferral item in this present budget which would permit a set-aside of these emergency cattle sales incomes on a tax-free base provided they are re-invested into cattle purchases, not at the end of the one year following as in this budget provision, but at the end of this current drought cycle?
I am proposing a form of special or personalized registered retirement savings plan. In this instance, however, the purpose is not for retirement purposes but for survival purposes. It must be something more than the basic herd provisions of pre-capital gains tax times in that more than the actual breeding herd emergency sales must be provided for through this method.
The prairie provincial governments already have the necessary provisions in their legislation to make their contribution by way of their provincial land tax authority. Crown grazing land rentals in both Alberta and Saskatchewan are determined by a formula that includes two variables; grass carrying capacity and the weighted average market price of grass cattle for the last half of the year based on Calgary for Alberta producers and Winnipeg for Saskatchewan producers.
Since grass carrying capacity has been reduced so drastically, especially in the short grass or chinook zones, in some cases it will be reduced to zero because of no stock water. The current lease rental rates should directly reflect this reduced carrying capacity.
Before leaving this drought issue, I think it is appropriate to remind all members of one of former President Harry Truman's well known quotes:
The only thing new is history we haven't read yet.
We should read and re-read the history of those ten drought years of the thirties. There is absolutely no reason why those same climatic conditions cannot return now, some 40 years

April 19, 1977
The Budget-Mr. Hargrave
later. We should be searching out people who were closely involved then, such as Dr. Asael Palmer, still living in retirement in Lethbridge. We should listen carefully to his words of wisdom after his lifetime of service with our federal agricultural research stations in southern Alberta.
Before I conclude, I want to make some general comments on our Canadian cattle industry. Several years from now when we look back and assess our cattle industry in 1976, it is my personal view that we will label 1976 as the worst year in our history for market prices, in relevant terms of course. I say this taking into consideration the dramatic increases in cost of production affecting every aspect of cattle production including cow-calf and yearling, the feeding side, and even seed stock or the purebred sector. I am now firmly convinced that the single most significant item contributing to last year's disastrous cattle price levels was the impact of those massive offshore beef imports from Australia and New Zealand.
About a year ago, at the start of the second quarter, there was a clear indication of a modest upturn in fed cattle prices in Canada. Some markets had shown increases of between $5 and $7 per hundredweight above the extreme low of market prices, and there was reason to believe this trend would continue throughout 1976. However, at the same time, about a year ago, the steady rise in offshore beef imports began and continued until year end. The Blue Book of the livestock and meat trade gives the following figures for the calendar year 1976. It shows that 188.5 million pounds of beef were imported from Australia and New Zealand. That is the equivalent of 535,000 live Canadian cows. By comparison, Canada marketed approximately 600,000 domestic cows in 1973 and 1974. Supplies of offshore beef represented an increase of 60 per cent over the 1975 level. More important still, these same offshore imports were on top of the largest domestic supply of beef in Canada's history.
That is not all, Mr. Speaker. Those imported supplies from down under were priced as much as 25 cents to 31 cents per pound below similar kinds of beef entering the U.S.A. from Australia and New Zealand. It was this situation which finally brought about the infamous "six cents under" rule proposed by the importers and agreed to by the Departments of Industry, Trade and Commerce and of Agriculture. Surely the rule begs the question: why should there be any discount at all?
The result of all this was that the modest upturn of a year ago collapsed, at least to the extent of $4 to $5 per hundredweight. Domestic cow prices were directly reduced by $3, and a further depressed fed cattle market continued until about two months ago. That cow market drop cost our industry $30 million and lowered its price structure to a point which permitted heavy exports of cows to the U.S.A.-110,000 head in 1975 and 187,000 head in 1976. All these developments were the result of the political decision made here in Ottawa to permit those massive offshore imports. The government's decision in mid-October, 1976, to impose import quotas, the day after the U.S. triggered its meat import law, was simply nine

months too late. The damage had been done-and what terrible damage it was to the entire Canadian cattle industry.
